name: ध्यानयोग
teaching: The mind must be befriended before it can be stilled: for the one who has conquered it, the mind is the closest ally; for the one who hasn't, it behaves like an enemy. Krishna gives the practice — seat, posture, moderation, patient return — and the image: a lamp in a windless place, unflickering. Even the practitioner who falls short loses nothing; no sincere effort on this path is ever wasted. The seat, the breath, the moderated life, the lamp in the windless place — meditation is given its complete manual, and then its safety net: no effort on this path is ever lost, across lifetimes. Its summit is the yogi who loves.
questions: Right now, is your mind your friend or your opponent?
Where is your life immoderate — in eating, sleeping, effort, rest — in ways that make stillness impossible?
Arjuna admits the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. What is your actual, daily relationship with practice and patience?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
अनाश्रितः कर्मफलं कार्यं कर्म करोति यः ।
स संन्यासी च योगी च न निरग्निर्न चाक्रियः॥
verses.transliteration:
anāśritaḥ karmaphalaṃ kāryaṃ karma karoti yaḥ
sa saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca na niragnirna cākriyaḥ
verses.essence: One who does the work that must be done without leaning on its fruit is the true sannyasi and yogi — not the one without fire or rites.
verses.translation: He who performs his bounden duty without depending on the fruits of his actions he is a Sannyasi and a Yogi; not he who is without fire and without action.

anvaya.base: आश्रित · resting on (आ + √श्रि · to lean on)
anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + आश्रित (leaning on): one who does not lean on
कर्म (action) + फल (fruit): the fruit of action

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be done), neuter, accusative singular

anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + अग्नि (fire): one who has given up the ritual fire
अ (not) + क्रिया (act): one who performs no acts

verses.explanation: The chapter opens by revoking renunciation's badges: no sacred fire, no rituals — these externals prove nothing. The double title goes instead to whoever still does the needful while no longer leaning on what it yields. Renunciation is measured at the point of motivation, not at the doorstep of the monastery.
verses.connection: Carries chapter 5's verdict forward: the working detached one holds both titles at once.
verses.reflection: Do one duty today expecting nothing back — and notice you have already begun renunciation.
verses.background: Chapter 6 opens with Krishna speaking unprompted. Śrīdhara says the chapter expands the yoga sketched at the end of chapter 5, and that this verse checks a hasty rush into renunciation, which the praise of knowledge and the painfulness of action might prompt, by ranking detached work above it.
verses.hook: What really makes someone a renunciant or a yogi?

views.text: Takes 'the work to be done' as the obligatory daily rites such as Agnihotra, and holds that the titles monk and yogi are given here only in a secondary sense: for giving up craving for results and for a mind kept undisturbed.

The worker treats his works as worship of the Supreme Person, wanting nothing from them but Him; so he holds both knowledge and action, whereas the one who merely drops the fires and rites has only knowledge.

Opens the chapter by saying that even a purified mind is not freed by renunciation alone without meditation; here karma-yoga is praised above a hasty renunciation. 'Without fire' means giving up fire-rites; 'without action' means giving up works done without fire.
Outward austerities like giving up fire or food do not make a renunciant or yogi. One who offers the fruits of action to God is the true renunciant and yogi, even while living with a family.

verses.devanagari:
यं संन्यासमिति प्राहुर्योगं तं विद्धि पाण्डव ।
न ह्यसंन्यस्तसङ्कल्पो योगी भवति कश्चन॥
verses.transliteration:
yaṃ saṃnyāsamiti prāhuryogaṃ taṃ viddhi pāṇḍava
na hyasaṃnyastasaṅkalpo yogī bhavati kaścana
verses.essence: What they call renunciation, know that as yoga, Pandava — for no one becomes a yogi without renouncing self-will.
verses.translation: Do thou, O Arjuna, know Yoga to be that which they call renunciation; no one verily becomes a Yogi who has not renounced thoughts.

anvaya.form: verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural

anvaya.meaning: one who has not dropped self-willed intentions
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + संन्यस्त (given up) + सङ्कल्प (intention): one whose intentions are not given up

verses.explanation: The two words are formally merged, and the common root is named: saṅkalpa — the mind's self-willed projecting of plans and cravings. Drop that, and renunciation and yoga turn out to be one act seen from two sides. What must be given up was never the work; it was the scheming around it.
verses.connection: Gives 6.1's double title its ground: no one becomes a yogi without giving up self-willed purpose, which is what renunciation means.
verses.reflection: Before one task today, notice your private plan for how it must turn out, and set it down. That letting-go is where yoga begins.
verses.background: Krishna has just given the working man the titles of renouncer and yogi. Śrīdhara frames this verse as the answer to the obvious "how so?": it names what renunciation and the yoga of action share, so the renouncer's name can fairly go to the one who works.
verses.hook: How are renunciation and yoga actually the same thing?

views.text: The likeness lies in the agent: the monk gives up all thought of actions and results, the karma-yogi gives up thought of results, which is what disturbs the mind. Karma-yoga is praised as renunciation because it is the remote aid to meditation.

Reads saṅkalpa as the delusion that the body is the self; only one who has dropped it by contemplating the self's true nature becomes a real karma-yogi, so karma-yoga already contains the knowledge called sannyasa.
Renunciation and yoga are ever interlinked: there is no renunciation without yoga, and no yoga without renouncing the intention for fruit.

Renunciation only stops the running toward the world; yoga carries the mind to God. A real renunciant unites the mind with God, and one cannot do so without dropping material desires, so each needs the other.

verses.devanagari:
आरुरुक्षोर्मुनेर्योगं कर्म कारणमुच्यते ।
योगारूढस्य तस्यैव शमः कारणमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
ārurukṣormuneryogaṃ karma kāraṇamucyate
yogārūḍhasya tasyaiva śamaḥ kāraṇamucyate
verses.essence: For the sage climbing toward yoga, action is the means; for the one who has reached yoga, serenity is the means.
verses.translation: For a sage who wishes to attain to Yoga, action is said to be the means; for the same sage who has attained to Yoga, inaction (quiescence) is said to be the means.

anvaya.form: desiderative adjective (wishing to), masculine, genitive singular (of/for)
verb, passive present, 3rd person singular (is said)

anvaya.meaning: for one who has climbed to yoga
anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + आरूढ (mounted): one who has mounted yoga

anvaya.form: verb, passive present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: One path, two gears. The climber needs karma — engagement that scrubs and steadies; the arrived needs śama — quiet that deepens what engagement built. The error is using the wrong gear for one's actual altitude: premature stillness stalls, perpetual busyness never summits.
verses.connection: Resolves the act-versus-sit tension as a question of stage, not of doctrine.
verses.reflection: Know your stage honestly today: still climbing needs action; arrived needs quiet. Prescribe accordingly.
verses.background: A doubt follows from 6.1–2: must one then keep to the yoga of action for life? Śrīdhara introduces this verse as Krishna setting its limit, saying when action serves the seeker and what takes its place once the height is reached.
verses.hook: Should a seeker keep working all life, or does a time for stillness come?

views.text: Śama means withdrawal from all actions: the more one withdraws from work, the more the self-controlled mind becomes concentrated, and then one is at once established in meditation.
Yoga here is the vision of the self; one keeps acting until that vision, and full release comes only when the body falls, so the vision is called release only by courtesy.
Quietude is the means of remaining uninterrupted at the stage already reached; the second 'cause' only points to that continuity rather than to a new attainment.
The right path depends on eligibility: beginners aspiring to yoga should practise karma yoga to purify the mind, while those already elevated can take up meditation and renunciation.

verses.devanagari:
यदा हि नेन्द्रियार्थेषु न कर्मस्वनुषज्जते ।
सर्वसङ्कल्पसंन्यासी योगारूढस्तदोच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā hi nendriyārtheṣu na karmasvanuṣajjate
sarvasaṅkalpasaṃnyāsī yogārūḍhastadocyate
verses.essence: When one clings neither to sense-objects nor to actions, having renounced all self-will, then one is called mounted on yoga.
verses.translation: When a man is not attached to the sense-objects or to actions, having renounced all thoughts, then he is said to have attained to Yoga.

anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + अर्थ (object): objects of the senses
सर्व (all) + सङ्कल्प (intention) + संन्यासिन् (renouncer): one who has given up all intentions

anvaya.meaning: one who has climbed to yoga
anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + आरूढ (mounted): one who has mounted yoga

anvaya.form: verb, passive present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: The summit-test for 6.3's gear-change: not just sense-objects released, but the subtler clinging to activity itself — the doer's addiction to doing. When both hooks are out and self-will has gone quiet, the climb is over and the sitting may rightly begin.
verses.connection: Gives the test for 6.3's 'one who has reached yoga', so no one turns to stillness before letting go of objects, actions and self-will.
verses.reflection: Mark a small milestone: one old craving that no longer argues when you pass it.
verses.background: Krishna has said that stillness is the means for one who has "climbed" to yoga, which leaves the question Śrīdhara puts at the head of this verse: what is the one mounted on yoga like? Here Krishna gives that person's mark.
verses.hook: How can you tell that someone has truly advanced in yoga?

views.text: Giving up all saṅkalpa means giving up all desires and so all actions, because desire springs from thought and action from desire; texts from Manu, the Mahabharata and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka are cited for this chain.
Detachment comes from a natural taste for experiencing the self; for one still drawn to sense-objects, karma-yoga practised as detachment from them is the way to climb.
Do not fight sense-objects head-on: think of God or the Self, and thinking of objects fades; since desires are born of thought, desires then die by themselves.
As the mind attaches to God, it detaches from the world. One is advanced when there is no craving for sense objects, no action to obtain them, and even memories of past enjoyment fade.

verses.devanagari:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् ।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः॥
verses.transliteration:
uddharedātmanātmānaṃ nātmānamavasādayet
ātmaiva hyātmano bandhurātmaiva ripurātmanaḥ
verses.essence: Let one lift the self by the self; let one not degrade the self. For the self alone is the self's friend, and the self alone its enemy.
verses.translation: One should raise oneself by one's Self alone; let not one lower oneself; for the Self alone is the friend of oneself, and the Self alone is the enemy of oneself.

anvaya.form: causative verb, optative, 3rd person singular (should make sink)

verses.explanation: The Gita's psychology in one couplet: no rescuer and no saboteur ultimately stands outside you. Uddhared ātmanātmānam — let one lift oneself by oneself. The same instrument — mind, will, habit — is rope or weight depending on how it is held: turned away from sense-objects it lifts, attached to them it sinks. Responsibility this total is alarming for a moment, then liberating: the decisive relationship of your life is already in the room, and no rescue arrives that the inner ally has not first agreed to.
verses.connection: Grounds the whole meditation chapter: before posture and breath, the self must take its own side.
verses.reflection: Lift yourself by yourself once today — one act your future self would thank you for, unprompted.
verses.background: The arrived yogi's mark has just been given: no clinging to sense-objects or actions. Śaṅkara says that once a person is so established, he is lifted from worldly life by his own self, and Krishna draws the lesson for everyone: responsibility for rising or sinking lies with oneself.
verses.hook: Who is ultimately responsible for lifting you up or dragging you down?

views.text: No other friend can free one from the world; an outer friend even binds through affection, and any outer enemy is ultimately of one's own making, so the emphatic 'alone' is justified.
The self that lifts is the mind: a mind unattached to sense-objects raises the self, while a mind still attached lets it sink in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Friends and enemies exist in the mind: the impure lower mind binds you and is your real enemy, the pure sattvic mind helps toward liberation and is your real friend.
We must walk the path ourselves; saints only guide. Having met saints in past lives without progress, we must accept responsibility, and recognise the mind as our greatest friend or greatest enemy.

verses.devanagari:
बन्धुरात्मात्मनस्तस्य येनात्मैवात्मना जितः ।
अनात्मनस्तु शत्रुत्वे वर्तेतात्मैव शत्रुवत्॥
verses.transliteration:
bandhurātmātmanastasya yenātmaivātmanā jitaḥ
anātmanastu śatrutve vartetātmaiva śatruvat
verses.essence: For one who has conquered the self, the self is a friend; for the unconquered, the self behaves like an enemy.
verses.translation: The Self is the friend of the self of him by whom the self has been conquered by the Self, but to the unconquered self, this Self stands in the position of an enemy, like an (external) foe.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (has been conquered)

anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + आत्मन् (self): one whose self is not mastered

verses.explanation: The condition on 6.5's friendship: it must be won. Bandhur ātmātmanas tasya — the same self is friend or foe by one variable, whether it has been conquered into alliance. An untrained mind is not neutral; it works against its owner śatruvat, like an enemy, sabotaging resolutions and amplifying fears. The unconquered mind does not merely fail you; it campaigns. The first conquest of any contemplative life is this internal alliance.
verses.connection: Sharpens 6.5: friend and enemy are not two selves but one self, before and after mastery.
verses.reflection: Check the alliance: is your mind working for you today, or running its own administration?
verses.background: Krishna has just declared that the self is its own friend and its own enemy. Śaṅkara poses the question this verse answers: what kind of self is one's friend, and what kind one's enemy?
verses.hook: When is your own mind a friend, and when is it an enemy?

refs.note: Hatred does not cease in those who dwell on thoughts of being insulted, hurt or robbed, showing how one's own mind becomes one's tormentor.

views.text: The self to be conquered is the aggregate of body and organs: brought under control they help concentration on the Self; left uncontrolled they act against one exactly as an outside enemy would.
The mind mastered with regard to sense-objects is a friend; unmastered, it works against one's highest good, as Parāśara says: the mind is the cause of both bondage and release.
There is no means here but one's own mind: subdued, it lifts one out of the dreadful round of birth and death; unsubdued, it acts as an enemy and throws one down.
Our worst enemies, lust, anger, greed and envy, live in our own mind and do more harm than outer foes. Brought under the intellect through spiritual practice, the same mind becomes our best friend.

verses.devanagari:
जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः ।
शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः॥
verses.transliteration:
jitātmanaḥ praśāntasya paramātmā samāhitaḥ
śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkheṣu tathā mānāpamānayoḥ
verses.essence: For the self-conquered and serene, the supreme Self stands steady — in cold and heat, joy and sorrow, honor and disgrace.
verses.translation: The Supreme Self of him who is self-controlled and peaceful is balanced in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as also in honour and dishonour.

anvaya.meaning: of one who has conquered himself
anvaya.parts: जित (conquered) + आत्मन् (self): one whose self is conquered
परम (highest) + आत्मन् (self)

anvaya.meaning: in cold, heat, pleasure and pain
anvaya.base: शीत · cold, उष्ण · heat, सुख · joy, दुःख · sorrow
anvaya.parts: शीत (cold) + उष्ण (heat) + सुख (pleasure) + दुःख (pain): a list joined by 'and'

anvaya.form: noun (compound), masculine, locative dual (in the two)
anvaya.parts: मान (honour) + अपमान (dishonour): the pair joined by 'and'

verses.explanation: What the won alliance feels like: an inner presence that no longer wobbles with the weather. The three test-pairs ascend in difficulty — body (cold-heat), feeling (joy-sorrow), and the hardest, social standing (honor-disgrace). Steadiness through the last is the rarest coin.
verses.connection: Shows 6.6's victory cashed out: the conquered self becomes a still platform for the Supreme.
verses.reflection: When you feel too hot or cold, or are praised or slighted today, notice the reaction and look for the part of you it does not reach.
verses.background: Following the friend-or-foe contrast of 6.5–6, Śrīdhara says Krishna now makes clear how the self is a friend to the one who has mastered it, turning to that person's state amid the pairs of opposites that unsettle everyone else.
verses.hook: How does a self-mastered person respond to heat and cold, praise and insult?

views.text: Samāhitaḥ means 'becomes manifest': for the calm, self-controlled monk the supreme Self becomes directly manifest as his own Self; the pairs of opposites describe how he should then remain even.
Paramātmā here is the individual self, called 'great' because of the context or its higher stage; or the phrase means 'the self is supremely composed'. It is not to be taken as the Supreme Being.
The calm one is the egoless one; his mind makes no difference between others and himself, and holds no like or dislike toward cold and heat and the other pairs.
The yogi who conquers the mind sees heat and cold, joy and sorrow as workings of the senses, separate from the soul, and stays unmoved; rising above dualities, the mind easily rests in God.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञानविज्ञानतृप्तात्मा कूटस्थो विजितेन्द्रियः ।
युक्त इत्युच्यते योगी समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः॥
verses.transliteration:
jñānavijñānatṛptātmā kūṭastho vijitendriyaḥ
yukta ityucyate yogī samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ
verses.essence: Content in knowledge and realization, unshakable, with senses subdued — such a yogi is called harnessed, to whom clod, stone and gold are alike.
verses.translation: The Yogi who is satisfied with the knowledge and the wisdom (of the Self), who has conquered the senses, and to whom a clod of earth, a piece of stone and gold are the same, is said to be harmonised (i.e., is said to have attained Nirvikalpa Samadhi).

anvaya.meaning: whose mind is fed by knowledge and realization
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + विज्ञान (realized knowledge) + तृप्त (satisfied) + आत्मन् (mind): one whose mind is satisfied with both
कूट (anvil, peak) + स्थ (standing): one who stays unchanged
विजित (fully conquered) + इन्द्रिय (senses): one whose senses are mastered

anvaya.form: verb, passive present, 3rd person singular (is said)

anvaya.meaning: to whom clod, stone and gold are equal
anvaya.parts: सम (equal) + लोष्ट (clod) + अश्मन् (stone) + काञ्चन (gold): one for whom these are alike

verses.explanation: Two kinds of knowing must both be present: jñāna, the learned map, and vijñāna, the terrain seen firsthand — contentment requires the second. Kūṭastha, anvil-still: the world hammers, the form holds. And the famous triad — dirt-clod, stone, gold — measures freedom by the wallet's loosened grip.
verses.connection: Continues the portrait of 6.7: inner steadiness shown against value itself.
verses.reflection: Look once at gold and once at gravel with the same eyes — just to feel what the sages feel.
verses.background: Krishna is closing his portrait of the one who has climbed to yoga, begun in 6.4. Śrīdhara calls this verse the summing-up of that person's marks and excellence. After cold and heat, honour and dishonour, it turns to his knowledge and to how he values things.
verses.hook: Why would a yogi see gold and a lump of earth as the same?

views.text: Jñāna is thorough knowledge of what scripture teaches; vijñāna is making those very things one's own direct realization, just as they were taught.

Vijñāna is knowing the self as different from matter (Prakṛti); kūṭastha means remaining the same self of pure knowledge through every birth as man or god. Such a karma-yogi is now fit for the yoga of self-vision.
Takes jñāna as knowledge free of falsehood, and vijñāna not as realization but as action that arises from varied, reasoned prior thought; the master of yoga is satisfied with both.
Kūṭastha is pictured as an anvil: iron is hammered and shaped on it, yet it stays unchanged; so the yogi stays unaffected though he meets sense-objects.
Illumined by both knowledge and realisation, the yogi sees all objects as modifications of God's material energy meant for His service, and so does not value things by their appeal.

verses.devanagari:
सुहृन्मित्रार्युदासीनमध्यस्थद्वेष्यबन्धुषु ।
साधुष्वपि च पापेषु समबुद्धिर्विशिष्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
suhṛnmitrāryudāsīnamadhyasthadveṣyabandhuṣu
sādhuṣvapi ca pāpeṣu samabuddhirviśiṣyate
verses.essence: One who is equal-minded toward well-wishers, friends, foes, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, kin, and toward saints and sinners alike — excels.
verses.translation: He who is of the same mind to the good-hearted, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful, the relatives, the righteous and the unrighteous, excels.

anvaya.meaning: toward every kind of friend, foe and kin
anvaya.base: सुहृद्, मित्र, अरि, उदासीन, मध्यस्थ, द्वेष्य, बन्धु
anvaya.parts: सुहृद् (well-wisher) + मित्र (friend) + अरि (foe) + उदासीन (indifferent) + मध्यस्थ (mediator) + द्वेष्य (the hateful) + बन्धु (relative): a list joined by 'and'
सम (equal) + बुद्धि (mind): one whose mind is the same toward all

anvaya.form: verb, passive present, 3rd person singular (is distinguished)

verses.explanation: The hardest equality: people. Nine categories — the whole social spectrum from the one who loves you to the one who hates you, from saint to sinner — met with sama-buddhi, an evenness of regard. Not blindness to difference, but a refusal to let difference dictate the heart's temperature.
verses.connection: Completes 6.7–8: equanimity proven against things, then against persons — the steeper slope.
verses.reflection: Apply one even-mindedness today across the hardest span: well-wisher, stranger, and someone who hurt you.
verses.background: Śaṅkara links it with "Further": the portrait goes on. Śrīdhara presents the verse as naming someone higher still than the yogi just described, and its opening line is a long graded list of the people one meets, from natural well-wishers to wrongdoers.
verses.hook: Can someone see friend, enemy and stranger with the same eye?

refs.note: The whole universe is pervaded by the Lord, grounding the highest equal vision that sees God in everyone.
Says the Supreme Person is all this, so everything is His energy.
Hanumān sees the whole world as filled with Sītā and Rāma.

views.text: The whole first line is one compound. Even-mindedness means the mind is not busy with who someone is and what he does; such a one is best among those established in yoga. A variant reading has vimucyate, 'becomes free'.

Defines each class closely, e.g. well-wishers regardless of age, friends of equal age, the hateful as hostile from birth. Since the self is yoga's only end and these people bring neither gain nor hindrance, he regards all equally as selves.
'He excels' means that stage after stage he goes out of the cycle of birth and death.
Equal vision has levels: seeing everyone as a soul, then God seated in everyone, and finally everyone as a form of God. The yogi with such vision toward all is even more elevated.

verses.devanagari:
योगी युञ्जीत सततमात्मानं रहसि स्थितः ।
एकाकी यतचित्तात्मा निराशीरपरिग्रहः॥
verses.transliteration:
yogī yuñjīta satatamātmānaṃ rahasi sthitaḥ
ekākī yatacittātmā nirāśīraparigrahaḥ
verses.essence: Let the yogi constantly discipline the self, remaining in solitude, alone, with mind and body controlled, free of longing and possession.
verses.translation: Let the Yogi try constantly to keep the mind steady, remaining in solitude, alone, with the mind and the body controlled, and free from hope and covetousness.

anvaya.parts: यत (controlled) + चित्त (mind) + आत्मन् (body, self): one whose mind and body are controlled
निर् (without) + आशिस् (wish): one without expectations
अ (not) + परिग्रह (possession): one who holds nothing

verses.explanation: The manual begins. Four conditions before a single breath of technique: solitude, aloneness (related but distinct — one can be solitary yet mentally crowded), restraint, and the two great unburdenings — no expectations, no holdings. Meditation starts by emptying the hands.
verses.connection: Opens the practical core (6.10–15): the portrait of 6.7–9 now taught as a discipline.
verses.reflection: Take ten minutes alone today — no phone, no audience, no inventory — and simply sit with yourself.
verses.background: The description of the arrived yogi is complete. Śrīdhara says Krishna now lays down the yoga itself with its parts, a teaching that runs to 'he is considered the highest yogi' (6.32). Still on the battlefield, Krishna speaks to Arjuna of practice in solitude.
verses.hook: What does someone need to begin a serious practice of meditation?

views.text: The words 'in a solitary place' and 'alone' imply that this discipline is undertaken after taking up monastic life, and even then with all acquisition given up.

The practitioner is a karma-yogi who daily sets aside time for the vision of the self; desirelessness means depending on nothing but the self, and non-possession means no sense of 'mine' toward anything else.
The yogi here is the one who has already climbed to yoga; nirāśīḥ can also be read as 'without food', alongside 'without longing'.
A householder can meditate in a quiet room at home; what matters is constancy, not fits and starts. With the senses truly withdrawn, one finds solitude even in a crowded city.

Mastery needs daily practice. Since worldly surroundings make the mind worldly, one should set aside time each day in seclusion for practice, like milk kept apart until it becomes butter that floats on water.

verses.devanagari:
शुचौ देशे प्रतिष्ठाप्य स्थिरमासनमात्मनः ।
नात्युच्छ्रितं नातिनीचं चैलाजिनकुशोत्तरम्॥
verses.transliteration:
śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiramāsanamātmanaḥ
nātyucchritaṃ nātinīcaṃ cailājinakuśottaram
verses.essence: In a clean place, having set a firm seat for oneself — neither too high nor too low — of cloth, deerskin and kusha grass.
verses.translation: In a clean spot, having established a firm seat of his own, neither too high nor too low, made of a cloth, a skin and Kusa-grass, one over the other.

anvaya.parts: अति (too) + उच्छ्रित (raised): excessively high
अति (too) + नीच (low): excessively low

anvaya.meaning: layered with cloth, skin and kusha grass
anvaya.parts: चैल (cloth) + अजिन (skin) + कुश (kusha grass) + उत्तर (laid over): a seat with these in layers

verses.explanation: The teaching descends, charmingly, to furniture — because the body's circumstances are the mind's first weather. Clean, stable, neither elevated (pride, precariousness) nor sunken (lethargy, damp): the middle height is already a metaphor the posture will repeat.
verses.connection: First of the concrete instructions: the outer seat prepared before the inner one.
verses.reflection: Prepare your seat with care tonight; the body honors what the hands arrange deliberately.
verses.background: The first of the practical rules. Śaṅkara lists what must now be covered: the seat, food and movement, the signs of success and the result. He says the seat comes first, and the verse leaves its sentence open, to be finished in 6.12.
verses.hook: What kind of seat and place should be prepared for meditation?

views.text: A clean spot is one pure in itself, not owned by impure persons and untouched by impure things; the seat itself is of wood or the like, covered with cloth, skin and kusha in reverse order.
Spread kusha grass on the ground, a deer or tiger skin over it, a cloth on top; sit on a naturally clean spot like a river bank, or clean the place where you meditate.
A clean place helps beginners keep the mind clean, and the layered seat insulates and protects. Where these details feel dated, keep their spirit: being absorbed in God matters most.

verses.devanagari:
तत्रैकाग्रं मनः कृत्वा यतचित्तेन्द्रियक्रियः ।
उपविश्यासने युञ्ज्याद्योगमात्मविशुद्धये॥
verses.transliteration:
tatraikāgraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā yatacittendriyakriyaḥ
upaviśyāsane yuñjyādyogamātmaviśuddhaye
verses.essence: There, making the mind one-pointed, with thought and senses controlled, seated on the seat, let one practice yoga for self-purification.
verses.translation: There, having made the mind one-pointed, with the actions of the mind and the senses controlled, let him, seated on the seat, practise Yoga for the purification of the self.

anvaya.parts: एक (one) + अग्र (point): having a single point

anvaya.meaning: with workings of mind and senses restrained
anvaya.parts: यत (restrained) + चित्त (mind) + इन्द्रिय (senses) + क्रिया (activity): one whose mental and sensory activity is held in check
आत्मन् (self, mind) + विशुद्धि (purification): purification of the self

verses.explanation: The aim is stamped on the practice before it starts: ātma-viśuddhaye, for purification — not for powers, visions, or even peace as a possession. Ekāgra, one-pointed: the mind's usual spray of attention gathered to a single beam. Everything that follows serves that gathering.
verses.connection: Names the motive that keeps 6.10–14's technique honest: cleansing, not acquiring.
verses.reflection: Sit once today on a steady seat and gather the mind to a single point for a few minutes, as cleaning, not achievement.
verses.background: Continues the sentence of 6.11: the seat is set, and the practitioner now sits on it. Śaṅkara, whose comment on both verses is given here, raises the question this verse settles: for what purpose should one concentrate the mind?
verses.hook: What should the meditator do with the mind once seated?

refs.note: Instructs the practitioner to be properly seated for spiritual practice, supporting the verse's guidance on posture.
Asks that one sit erect and still, matching the verse's instruction to hold body, head and neck steady.
Patañjali says the meditation posture should be steady and comfortable, so any seat one can hold motionless will serve.

views.text: Self-purification means purification of the internal organ; the mind is made one-pointed by withdrawing it from all objects.
The yoga practised here is the vision of the self, and its purifying aim is the ending of bondage.
When you first sit, old thoughts and memories rush up as if the lid of the subconscious were lifted; do not be discouraged, and keep strict regularity.

Sitting erect and still guards against drowsiness, and any posture one can hold motionlessly will do, even a chair. Meditation is an inner journey that purifies the mind, and it is best when focused on God.

verses.devanagari:
समं कायशिरोग्रीवं धारयन्नचलं स्थिरः ।
सम्प्रेक्ष्य नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन्॥
verses.transliteration:
samaṃ kāyaśirogrīvaṃ dhārayannacalaṃ sthiraḥ
samprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaścānavalokayan
verses.essence: Holding body, head and neck erect and still, gazing at the tip of the nose, not looking around —
verses.translation: Let him firmly hold his body, head and neck erect and still, gazing at the tip of his nose, without looking around.

anvaya.base: काय · trunk, शिरस् · head, ग्रीवा · neck
anvaya.parts: काय (trunk) + शिरस् (head) + ग्रीवा (neck): the three taken as one unit

anvaya.form: present participle (while holding), masculine, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: नासिका (nose) + अग्र (tip): the tip of the nose

anvaya.form: present participle, negated (while not looking), masculine, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The spine as plumb-line: body, head, neck stacked sama, even — alertness built into architecture. The nose-tip gaze is a leash for the eyes, the most restless of the senses; diśaś cānavalokayan, no glancing at the directions, closes the world's ten doors of distraction.
verses.connection: The posture of 6.11–12 completed upward: stillness made structural.
verses.reflection: Hold the spine quietly tall for two minutes; let posture teach steadiness to the mind.
verses.background: With the seat established, Śaṅkara says Krishna now states how the body should be held. The verse gives only the bodily half of the instruction; its sentence runs on into 6.14 for the inner bearing and the main verb.
verses.hook: How should the body and eyes be held during meditation?

refs.note: Instructs the practitioner to be properly seated for spiritual practice, supporting the verse's guidance on posture.
Asks that one sit erect and still, matching the verse's instruction to hold body, head and neck steady.
Patañjali says the meditation posture should be steady and comfortable, so any seat one can hold motionless will serve.

views.text: The nose-tip is looked at only 'as it were': the instruction is to withdraw the gaze from outer objects, not to fix the mind on the nose, since the mind is to rest on the Self.
'Body' here means the trunk; body, head and neck are held straight from the base of the spine to the crown, and the nose-tip gaze implies half-closed eyes.
Master the posture by daily practice until you are as firm as a statue; direct the gaze gently, never straining the eyes.

Sitting erect and still guards against drowsiness, and any posture one can hold motionlessly will do, even a chair. Meditation is an inner journey that purifies the mind, and it is best when focused on God.

verses.devanagari:
प्रशान्तात्मा विगतभीर्ब्रह्मचारिव्रते स्थितः ।
मनः संयम्य मच्चित्तो युक्त आसीत मत्परः॥
verses.transliteration:
praśāntātmā vigatabhīrbrahmacārivrate sthitaḥ
manaḥ saṃyamya maccitto yukta āsīta matparaḥ
verses.essence: Serene, fearless, firm in the vow of brahmacharya, with mind restrained and thinking of me, let one sit harnessed, holding me supreme.
verses.translation: Serene-minded, fearless, firm in the vow of a Brahmachari, having controlled the mind, thinking of Me and balanced in mind, let him sit, having Me as his supreme goal.

anvaya.parts: प्रशान्त (calm) + आत्मन् (mind): one whose mind is at peace
विगत (gone) + भी (fear): one whose fear has gone

anvaya.meaning: in the vow of the celibate student
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्मचारिन् (celibate student) + व्रत (vow): the brahmacharya vow
मद् (me) + चित्त (thought): one whose mind is on me
मद् (me) + पर (supreme): one for whom I am the supreme goal

verses.explanation: The inner posture to match the outer: serenity, and — easy to miss — vigata-bhīḥ, fearlessness, for the silence of meditation surfaces what noise kept down. Then the object: mat-paraḥ, me as the highest. The Gita's meditation is not on emptiness but on a Person; attention needs a home, and the home offered is Krishna.
verses.connection: Crowns the technique: seat, posture and gaze were scaffolding; the dwelling-place is Him.
verses.reflection: Sit for a few minutes today with your fears set aside, the mind held in, and your thought resting on the highest you know.
verses.background: Completes the sentence of 6.13. Body, head and gaze have been set; this verse adds the inner bearing and the command itself, "let him sit." For the first time in these instructions, Krishna names himself as the one on whom the mind should rest.
verses.hook: What inner attitude and focus does successful meditation need?

refs.note: Patañjali says that firmness in celibacy brings great vigour, supporting the verse's call to keep the vow of celibacy.
Lists eight sex-related activities, from thinking about it to engaging in it, that celibacy requires one to give up.

views.text: The celibate's vow includes serving the teacher and living on alms. A passionate man may think of a woman yet hold the king as his goal; this yogi has Me as both the object of thought and the supreme goal.
The closing words are a direct instruction: sit in yoga concentrating on Krishna alone.
Fearlessness is the most important qualification; and brahmacharya, as continence that preserves vital energy, is the foundation for long, steady meditation.
Celibacy, understood as restraint in thought, speech and deed, is essential for meditation and brings energy and clarity. The object of meditation must be God alone.

verses.devanagari:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी नियतमानसः ।
शान्तिं निर्वाणपरमां मत्संस्थामधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
yuñjannevaṃ sadātmānaṃ yogī niyatamānasaḥ
śāntiṃ nirvāṇaparamāṃ matsaṃsthāmadhigacchati
verses.essence: Thus ever harnessing the self, the yogi of disciplined mind attains the peace that culminates in nirvana and abides in me.
verses.translation: Thus always keeping the mind balanced, the Yogi, with the mind controlled, attains to the peace abiding in Me, which culminates in liberation.

anvaya.form: present participle (while doing), masculine, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: नियत (controlled) + मानस (mind): one whose mind is controlled
निर्वाण (liberation) + परम (highest): whose highest point is nirvana
मद् (me) + संस्था (abiding): that which rests in me

verses.explanation: The practice section closes with its destination, and the destination has an address: śāntiṁ... mat-saṁsthām — a peace that doesn't trail off into the abstract but settles *in me*. Nirvana, the great extinguishing, turns out to be an arrival as much as a cessation. Note sadā: not a retreat's worth of yoga but a life's.
verses.connection: Seals 6.10–14 with the promise — peace whose far edge is union.
verses.reflection: Practice small but practice always; nirvana is built of ordinary, repeated sittings.
verses.background: The instructions on seat, posture and mind are finished. Śaṅkara introduces this verse as the statement of yoga's result, and says that after it Krishna turns to the rules about the yogi's food and sleep.
verses.hook: What peace does steady meditation on the Lord finally lead to?

refs.note: Says God's name is even greater than God in what it gives souls, supporting meditation on the name.

views.text: The peace attained is indifference to worldly attachments and possessions, which culminates in liberation.
The mind is fixed on the Supreme Person as the holy, auspicious object of meditation; contact with Him is what purifies and steadies the yogi's mind.
'Always' means not for a limited period; the peace that arises is one whose culmination is the same as attaining Me.

Meditation should purify the mind, which only happens by fixing it on God, who is all-pure. One may meditate on His names, forms, virtues and pastimes, or serve Him in the mind; this leads to liberation.

verses.devanagari:
नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः ।
न चातिस्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन॥
verses.transliteration:
nātyaśnatastu yogo'sti na caikāntamanaśnataḥ
na cātisvapnaśīlasya jāgrato naiva cārjuna
verses.essence: Yoga is not for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who fasts to extremes; not for the over-sleeper, Arjuna, nor for the ever-wakeful.
verses.translation: Verily Yoga is not possible for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all, nor for him who sleeps too much, nor for him who is (always) awake, O Arjuna.

anvaya.meaning: for one who eats too much
anvaya.parts: अति (too much) + अश्नत् (eating): over-eating

anvaya.meaning: for one who does not eat
anvaya.form: present participle, negated, masculine, genitive singular (of/for)
anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + अश्नत् (eating): not eating

anvaya.meaning: for one given to too much sleep
anvaya.parts: अति (too much) + स्वप्न (sleep) + शील (habit): one habitually oversleeping

verses.explanation: A verse of immense kindness to the body: four extremes disqualified, two of them ascetic. Heroic fasting and vigil are rejected as firmly as indulgence — both are violence to the instrument, and a damaged instrument plays no music. The Gita's yoga refuses to be impressed by self-harm.
verses.connection: Pre-empts the zealot's misreading of 6.10–15: discipline, yes; mortification, no.
verses.reflection: Check your extremes today: too much food or none, too much sleep or none — yoga lives between.
verses.background: Having given the result, Krishna adds rules for the yogi's daily life. Śrīdhara takes this verse and the next together as one rule about food and the like, this one stating it by the extremes that rule yoga out. Krishna addresses Arjuna by name.
verses.hook: Can eating or sleeping too much, or too little, block your practice?

refs.note: Those who pursue only material knowledge and those devoted only to spiritual knowledge both fall into darkness, so both must be balanced.
Calls the body the instrument for practising dharma, so it must be cared for.
Says the Vedas do not ask one to neglect the body in spiritual life.

views.text: Eat what is within one's capacity: more harms, less does not sustain. Yoga texts give the measure: half the stomach for food, a quarter for water, a quarter left for air.
Extends the rule beyond food and sleep: excessive recreation and none at all, overwork and idleness, are equally opposed to yoga.
We are not the body, yet it carries us and must be cared for; illness hinders practice. Balanced diet, exercise and sleep are part of Vedic knowledge, so extremes in either direction obstruct yoga.

verses.devanagari:
युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु ।
युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा॥
verses.transliteration:
yuktāhāravihārasya yuktaceṣṭasya karmasu
yuktasvapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkhahā
verses.essence: For one moderate in food and recreation, moderate in effort in actions, moderate in sleep and waking — yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
verses.translation: Yoga becomes the destroyer of pain for him who is moderate in eating and recreation (such as walking, etc.), who is moderate in exertion in actions, who is moderate in sleep and wakefulness.

anvaya.meaning: of one moderate in food and recreation
anvaya.parts: युक्त (moderate) + आहार (food) + विहार (recreation): one whose eating and movement are measured
युक्त (moderate) + चेष्टा (effort): one whose effort is measured

anvaya.meaning: of one moderate in sleep and waking
anvaya.parts: युक्त (moderate) + स्वप्न (sleep) + अवबोध (waking): one whose sleep and waking are regulated
दुःख (sorrow) + हन् (slayer): that which destroys sorrow

verses.explanation: The positive law after 6.16's prohibitions: yukta three times — measured, fitted, tuned. Eating, playing, working, sleeping: the whole round of an ordinary day calibrated to the middle. And only on that humble foundation does the grand promise stand: duḥkha-hā, sorrow-slayer. Transcendence rests on schedule.
verses.connection: The other half of 6.16's rule: after the extremes that rule yoga out, the moderation in food, rest, effort and sleep that lets yoga end sorrow.
verses.reflection: Tune one habit toward moderation today and watch how much pain was self-scheduled.
verses.background: Having said for whom yoga is impossible, Krishna is left with the question Śaṅkara puts before this verse: how, then, does yoga become possible? The answer is the positive half of the rule begun in 6.16, covering food, recreation, effort and sleep.
verses.hook: How does moderation in daily habits help end suffering?

views.text: 'Food' (āhāra) means everything gathered in, and 'recreation' means moving about; when these, effort in work, and sleep and waking are all regulated, Yoga destroys every worldly sorrow.
Takes 'food' as the sense-objects the senses bring in, and 'effort' as the activity of enjoying them; the right measure is neither unlimited indulgence nor unlimited abstention.
Austerity is a means, not the goal, and becomes harmful as self-torture; keep a regular routine of measured food and fixed hours of sleep and rising.

Indulgence violates the body's laws and leads to disease, which blocks yoga. Being temperate in eating, recreation, work and sleep, as the Buddha's middle path later echoed, frees one from bodily and mental sorrow.

verses.devanagari:
यदा विनियतं चित्तमात्मन्येवावतिष्ठते ।
निःस्पृहः सर्वकामेभ्यो युक्त इत्युच्यते तदा॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā viniyataṃ cittamātmanyevāvatiṣṭhate
niḥspṛhaḥ sarvakāmebhyo yukta ityucyate tadā
verses.essence: When the disciplined mind rests in the Self alone, free of longing for any desire, then one is said to be harnessed.
verses.translation: When the perfectly controlled mind rests in the Self only, free from longing for all the objects of desires, then it is said, 'He is united'.

anvaya.parts: निस् (without) + स्पृहा (longing): one without craving
सर्व (all) + काम (desire): all desires

anvaya.form: verb, passive present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: The checkpoint: the mind no longer pacing its cage but settled — avatiṣṭhate, taking up residence — in the Self. The test is niḥspṛha, the absence of that low hum of wanting that usually runs beneath all thought. When the hum stops, the word yukta finally applies.
verses.connection: Defines arrival for the practice of 6.10–17, before the famous image that pictures it.
verses.reflection: Notice one moment today when you want nothing at all, and stay in it a little before the next wish arrives.
verses.background: The rules of practice are given. Śrīdhara introduces the verse with the question it answers: when is a person's yoga accomplished? Krishna now defines the point at which a practitioner may be called "united," the term the chapter keeps using.
verses.hook: When is a person said to be truly established in yoga?

views.text: The mind, made fully one-pointed, rests in the non-dual Self alone; the longing given up covers objects both seen and unseen, of this world and the next.
The mind settles because it finds unsurpassable good in the self alone; 'yukta' here means fit for yoga.
Yoga is complete when the controlled mind is fixed on God alone; then it is automatically freed from sense cravings, and the person is called united.

verses.devanagari:
यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता ।
योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः॥
verses.transliteration:
yathā dīpo nivātastho neṅgate sopamā smṛtā
yogino yatacittasya yuñjato yogamātmanaḥ
verses.essence: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the likeness recalled of the yogi of disciplined mind, absorbed in the yoga of the Self.
verses.translation: As a lamp placed in a windless spot does not flicker to such is compared the Yogi of controlled mind, practising Yoga in the Self (or absorbed in the Yoga of the Self).

anvaya.parts: निवात (windless place) + स्थ (standing): placed out of the wind

anvaya.meaning: of one whose mind is controlled
anvaya.parts: यत (controlled) + चित्त (mind): one whose mind is restrained

anvaya.meaning: of the Self, on the Self

verses.explanation: Yathā dīpo nivāta-sthaḥ — as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker: the image the meditation tradition took as its emblem. The flame is not put out — awareness burns at full brightness — only the flickering stops, because the wind of desire and distraction has been stilled. Steadiness without dimming: alertness and peace, finally in the same body. The practice is less about strengthening the flame than about finding, or building, the windless room.
verses.connection: Pictures the mind 6.18 just defined: the settled yogi is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker.
verses.reflection: Find your windless place today — the corner of the day where the flame of attention stops flickering.
verses.background: The settled mind has just been defined. Śaṅkara introduces this verse as an illustration offered for the mind of the absorbed yogi. It is the chapter's one image, and Krishna presents it as a comparison already known to those who understand yoga.
verses.hook: What does a mind steady in meditation look like?

views.text: The simile is one 'thought of' by knowers of yoga who understand the movements of the mind; it pictures the mind of the yogi engaged in absorption in the Self.
The flame is steady but still shining: when all other mental activity ceases, the self remains with its steady light of knowledge.
The 'flickering' that stops is the yogi's effort to acquire sense-objects and the like.
Like a flame in a windless place, the yogi's mind, held in loving union with God, is sheltered from the winds of desire and stays steady by the power of devotion.

verses.devanagari:
यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया ।
यत्र चैवात्मनात्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
yatroparamate cittaṃ niruddhaṃ yogasevayā
yatra caivātmanātmānaṃ paśyannātmani tuṣyati
verses.essence: Where the mind comes to rest, restrained by the practice of yoga, and where, beholding the Self by the self, one is content in the Self —
verses.translation: When the mind, restrained by the practice of Yoga attains to quietude and when seeing the Self by the self, he is satisfied in his own Self.

anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + सेवा (practice): practice of yoga

anvaya.form: present participle (while seeing), masculine, nominative singular

verses.explanation: A four-verse definition of the goal begins. First mark: uparamate, the mind doesn't just slow — it comes to rest, the way water stills when the stirring stops. In that stillness the impossible-sounding event occurs: the self sees the Self, awareness catching its own light, and contentment needs no further object.
verses.connection: Begins the great description (6.20–23) of what the windless lamp actually illuminates.
verses.reflection: Touch the moment in stillness where the self, seeing itself, is quietly satisfied.
verses.background: Śrīdhara notes that "yoga" meant action in 6.2 but absorption in 6.16, and asks which is yoga in the main sense. Krishna answers in three and a half verses defining absorption by its nature and fruit; this verse opens that long sentence with "where."
verses.hook: What does a person discover when the mind becomes completely still?

views.text: The Self seen here is by nature the supreme light of Consciousness, and it is seen by the mind purified through concentration; one is then content in that Self alone.
Reads 6.20–23 as one sentence, takes uparamate as 'rejoices' in surpassing felicity, and ends with the definition of yoga as disunion from all union with pain.
Yoga in its main sense is samādhi, defined here by its nature, as in Patañjali's 'yoga is the stilling of the mind's modifications', and by its fruit, seeing the Self and being content.
A purified mind is like muddy water cleared with alum: once the dirt settles, the soul is perceived directly as distinct from body, mind and intellect, beyond mere theory.

verses.devanagari:
सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद् बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम् ।
वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वतः॥
verses.transliteration:
sukhamātyantikaṃ yattad buddhigrāhyamatīndriyam
vetti yatra na caivāyaṃ sthitaścalati tattvataḥ
verses.essence: Where one knows that boundless happiness which is grasped by the understanding, beyond the senses — and established there, never strays from the truth —
verses.translation: When he (the Yogi) feels that Infinite Bliss which can be grasped by the (pure) intellect and which transcends the senses, and established wherein he never moves from the Reality.

anvaya.base: बुद्धिग्राह्य · to be grasped by intellect
anvaya.parts: बुद्धि (intellect) + ग्राह्य (to be grasped): that which is grasped by the intellect
अति (beyond) + इन्द्रिय (sense organ): that which lies beyond the senses

verses.explanation: Second mark: a happiness with strange specifications — atīndriya, off the sensory grid entirely, yet buddhi-grāhya, apprehensible by the refined understanding. Most joy is delivered through the senses and leaves with them; this one is met by a deeper faculty and therefore cannot be confiscated.
verses.connection: Names the positive content of 6.20's rest: not blankness but trans-sensory bliss.
verses.reflection: Trust the joy beyond the senses once felt — let one taste of depth recalibrate all your sweets.
verses.background: The second clause of the long sentence begun in 6.20. Śrīdhara reads it as giving the reason the yogi is content in the Self, and meets the objection it raises: with the senses cut off from their objects, where could any happiness come from?
verses.hook: What kind of joy lies beyond the senses, and does it last?

refs.note: God is bliss itself; the soul becomes blissful on attaining Him, the joy beyond the senses the verse describes.
Identifies the Supreme as made of bliss.
Describes God's forms as made of eternity, knowledge and bliss.

views.text: The bliss is infinite and intuited by the intellect alone, without the senses, so it is not an object; established in the nature of the Self, the illumined one never deviates from Reality.
The bliss is grasped only by an intellect contemplating the self; the yogi does not swerve from that state simply because the happiness it gives is overwhelming.
Meets an objection: how can there be joy with no contact of senses and objects? The bliss is beyond that contact and is grasped by the intellect alone as it takes the form of the Self.
In deep meditation the senses stop working and are drawn back into the mind; the intellect, purified by restraints, observances and steady meditation, then grasps the Self's bliss.

The soul longs for bliss because it is part of God, the ocean of bliss. Sense pleasures give only a shadow of it; in union with God, in samādhi, the soul tastes complete bliss and stays fixed in the Truth.

verses.devanagari:
यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं ततः ।
यस्मिन्स्थितो न दुःखेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yaṃ labdhvā cāparaṃ lābhaṃ manyate nādhikaṃ tataḥ
yasminsthito na duḥkhena guruṇāpi vicālyate
verses.essence: Gaining which, one reckons no other gain greater; established in which, one is not shaken even by the heaviest sorrow —
verses.translation: Which, having obtained, he thinks there is no other gain superior to it; wherein established, he is not moved even by heavy sorrow.

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, instrumental singular (by), describing दुःखेन
verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done to him)

verses.explanation: Third mark, the double test: against all possible gains, this one ends the search — the comparing mind retires; and against guru duḥkha, grief of the heaviest grade, it holds. Not painlessness — the Gita never promises that — but unshakenness: sorrow arrives and finds no purchase on the foundation.
verses.connection: The goal of 6.20–21 stress-tested at both extremes — supreme gain, supreme loss.
verses.reflection: Recall your steadiest moment and ask: established there, what calamity could really move me?
verses.background: The third clause of the sentence running from 6.20. Śrīdhara says it establishes the steadiness just claimed for the yogi, and that yoga is here also marked by its fruit: the end of what one dreads, as well as the gaining of what one wants.
verses.hook: Is there a gain after which even great sorrow cannot shake you?

views.text: Having gained this Self-attainment, one counts no other gain higher, and, established in the Reality of the Self, is unshaken even by great sorrow such as being struck by weapons.
Even after waking from yoga he longs for that state alone and counts nothing else a gain; the heaviest sorrow meant is grief like losing a virtuous son.
Reads 'not shaken much': a slight, momentary stir may remain from old impressions or from compassion for beings, but never the despair of 'I am undone'.
Pain is felt only when one identifies with body and mind; like a patient under chloroform, the one resting in the Self is untouched by it.
No worldly gain satisfies, since something higher always remains. God's bliss is infinite and eternal, so one who attains it feels the goal is reached and, like Prahlāda, stays unshaken by any trial.

verses.devanagari:
तं विद्याद् दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम् ।
स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा॥
verses.transliteration:
taṃ vidyād duḥkhasaṃyogaviyogaṃ yogasaṃjñitam
sa niścayena yoktavyo yogo'nirviṇṇacetasā
verses.essence: Know that as yoga: the unyoking from union with sorrow. It must be practiced with resolve, with a mind undismayed.
verses.translation: Let that be known by the name of Yoga, the severance from union with pain. This Yoga should be practised with determination and with an undesponding mind.

anvaya.base: दुःखसंयोगवियोग · severance from contact with pain
anvaya.parts: दुःख (pain) + संयोग (contact, union) + वियोग (separation): the separation from contact with pain
योग (yoga) + संज्ञित (named): that which bears the name yoga

anvaya.form: gerundive, masculine, nominative singular (must be done)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + निर्विण्ण (dejected, weary) + चेतस् (mind): a mind that is not dejected

verses.explanation: The chapter's definitional jewel, built on a pun: yoga, 'union', defined as viyoga, 'dis-union' — the surgical separation from our oldest attachment, the one to suffering itself. Then two clinical instructions for the long operation: niścaya, settled resolve, and anirviṇṇa-cetas — a heart that has renounced discouragement.
verses.connection: Caps 6.20–22 by naming the whole achievement, and pivots to the labor it costs.
verses.reflection: Redefine yoga today as Krishna does: the unlinking from your link with sorrow. Practice with resolve.
verses.background: The "where…" clauses of 6.20–22 reach their main statement in this verse's first half; Śaṅkara links it back to the state described from 6.20. The second half then adds how this yoga must be undertaken.
verses.hook: What is yoga, if it is defined by what it frees you from?

refs.note: Kṛṣṇa is like the sun and Māyā like darkness; where Kṛṣṇa is, Māyā has no power, so union with God ends misery.

views.text: This is a definition by negation: yoga is known as the severance of contact with sorrow. Perseverance and an undepressed heart are then named as the disciplines for reaching it.
'Undepressed' can mean the mind no longer sinks because the goal is reached, or, taken the other way, the mind depressed at how firm and painful the cycle of birth and death is.

Calling separation 'yoga' is a deliberate naming by opposites; properly yoga joins the individual soul to the Supreme. Despondency means slackening effort because practice feels painful; resolve comes from scripture and teacher.
Yoga means both attaining God's bliss and freedom from the misery of Māyā; when God's light enters the heart, Māyā's darkness cannot remain. This perfection comes only through determined practice.

verses.devanagari:
सङ्कल्पप्रभवान्कामांस्त्यक्त्वा सर्वानशेषतः ।
मनसैवेन्द्रियग्रामं विनियम्य समन्ततः॥
verses.transliteration:
saṅkalpaprabhavānkāmāṃstyaktvā sarvānaśeṣataḥ
manasaivendriyagrāmaṃ viniyamya samantataḥ
verses.essence: Abandoning without remainder all desires born of self-will, restraining the host of senses from every side with the mind —
verses.translation: Abandoning without reserve all desires born of Sankalpa (thought and imagination) and completely restraining the whole group of the senses by the mind from all sides.

anvaya.parts: सङ्कल्प (willing, mental plan) + प्रभव (origin): those whose origin is saṅkalpa
इन्द्रिय (sense) + ग्राम (village, group): the senses taken as one crowd

verses.explanation: The method resumes with its hardest clause: aśeṣataḥ, without remainder — desires kept as souvenirs regrow. Their source is named: saṅkalpa, the mind's plan-making, whose renunciation 6.2 and 6.4 already demanded; cut the projector and the films stop. Indriya-grāma, the senses as a village — restless, many-voiced, governed only patiently and from every gate.
verses.connection: Resumes practice after the goal-vision: what 6.23's resolve actually does, hour by hour.
verses.reflection: Abandon one desire completely today — root and branch — and rein one sense by mind alone.
verses.background: Krishna has just said that yoga must be practised with resolve. Śrīdhara reads this verse as tied to that very command, "yoga should be practised," so its clauses spell out how: first desire, then the senses. Its sentence continues into 6.25.
verses.hook: What is the first step in turning the mind away from the world?

views.text: Separates two kinds of desire: those from sense contact like heat and cold, which cannot be avoided, and mind-made ones for sons or land, which can be dropped; for the first, drop only the sense of pleasure and pain.
'By the mind alone' means the restraint is inward: it is not achieved by withdrawing from activities.

The mind cleverly keeps a few desires for secret enjoyment, so renounce without reservation; destroy the imagining first and desires die by themselves, while one unruly sense is enough to scatter the mind.

Meditation first removes the mind from the world. Thoughts grow into pursuit and aversion, then desire, which block meditation, so one must give up attachment to material objects and restrain the senses.

verses.devanagari:
शनैः शनैरुपरमेद् बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया ।
आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किञ्चिदपि चिन्तयेत्॥
verses.transliteration:
śanaiḥ śanairuparamed buddhyā dhṛtigṛhītayā
ātmasaṃsthaṃ manaḥ kṛtvā na kiñcidapi cintayet
verses.essence: Little by little let one withdraw, with understanding held in steadiness; making the mind abide in the Self, let one think of nothing at all.
verses.translation: Little by little let him attain to quietude by the intellect held firmly; having made the mind establish itself in the Self, let him not think of anything.

anvaya.parts: धृति (steadiness) + गृहीत (held): held firm by steadiness
आत्मन् (Self) + संस्थ (abiding): resting in the Self

verses.explanation: Two words save a thousand meditators: śanaiḥ śanaiḥ, slowly, slowly. The mind is not slammed shut but settled by degrees, the way sediment sinks in undisturbed water. Dhṛti-gṛhītayā — the understanding held by patience — and then the summit instruction, stated with disarming simplicity: think of nothing at all.
verses.connection: The tempo-marking for 6.24's restraint: gradual is not a concession but the method itself.
verses.reflection: Withdraw little by little this evening; let the mind settle in the Self and think of nothing else.
verses.background: Continues the instruction of 6.24: with desires dropped and senses reined in, the mind itself must be brought to rest. Śrīdhara frames it as the remedy if the momentum of past habit still makes the mind waver: steady it by holding firm, step by step.
verses.hook: Does the mind settle at once, or step by step?

views.text: The mind is fixed in the Self with the thought 'the Self alone is all, nothing exists apart from it'; then nothing else is thought. This is called the highest instruction on yoga.
Rejects the reading 'think only the void' as leading to nihilism; 'think of nothing' means not dwelling on taking up or giving up objects.
If old karmic impressions shake the mind, steady it by concentration, slowly and not by force; once still, the yogi shines as supreme bliss and need not even turn away from meditating on the Self.
After withdrawing from the world, the mind must be fixed on God, which happens slowly by determined effort. A firm intellect convinced of the world's impermanence gradually turns the senses back.

verses.devanagari:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् ।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत्॥
verses.transliteration:
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram
tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet
verses.essence: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders out, from there reining it in, let one bring it under the sway of the Self alone.
verses.translation: From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that let him restrain it and bring it under the control of the Self alone.
verses.explanation: The most practically merciful verse in the chapter: yato yataḥ... tatas tataḥ — wherever it wanders, from there. The wandering is assumed, budgeted for, not condemned; the practice is the return, performed ten thousand times without drama. Two verbs share the work: niyamya, rein it in, and ātmany eva vaśaṃ nayet, lead it back under the Self's sway. Meditation, defined here, is not the absence of distraction but the patience of retrieval. The returning is the meditation; the wandering merely supplies occasions.
verses.connection: The working loop inside 6.25's slowness: stray, notice, return — the whole technique.
verses.reflection: Each time attention wanders today, bring it back without commentary — that returning is the exercise.
verses.background: Even with steady holding, the mind may still slip out, restless by nature and driven by passion. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as Krishna's instruction for that case, the practical companion to the command of 6.25 to think of nothing.
verses.hook: What should you do each time the mind wanders off?

views.text: Restrain the mind from sound and the other objects by seeing through discrimination that they are mere appearances, with detachment; by the power of practice the mind merges in the Self.
The mind strays because of its pull toward sense objects; it is brought back with effort by contemplating the incomparable bliss within the self.
Like a bull that runs off and is dragged home, then fed treats so it stays, the mind must be pulled back and given a taste of the Self's bliss until it no longer runs out.

Withdrawing the mind from the world and placing it on God take effort, while its wandering back happens by itself. Do not lose heart; repeat the two steps again and again until attachment to God grows.

verses.devanagari:
प्रशान्तमनसं ह्येनं योगिनं सुखमुत्तमम् ।
उपैति शान्तरजसं ब्रह्मभूतमकल्मषम्॥
verses.transliteration:
praśāntamanasaṃ hyenaṃ yoginaṃ sukhamuttamam
upaiti śāntarajasaṃ brahmabhūtamakalmaṣam
verses.essence: Supreme bliss comes to this yogi of peaceful mind, with passion stilled — become Brahman, free of stain.
verses.translation: Supreme Bliss verily comes to this Yogi whose mind is quite peaceful, whose passion is quieted, who has become Brahman and who is free from sin.

anvaya.meaning: whose mind is fully at peace
anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, accusative singular (describing the yogi)
anvaya.parts: प्रशान्त (fully calmed) + मनस् (mind): one whose mind is fully calm
शान्त (stilled) + रजस् (passion, restlessness): one whose rajas has been stilled
ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) + भूत (become): one who has become Brahman
अ (not) + कल्मष (stain, sin): one without stain

verses.explanation: Note the verb's direction: upaiti — the bliss *comes to* the yogi. Happiness was never manufactured by the practice; the practice only quieted the turbulence (śānta-rajasam) that kept it at bay. Still the water, and the moon that was always overhead appears in it.
verses.connection: The fruit of 6.26's patient returns: what arrives on its own when the chasing stops.
verses.reflection: Catch the supreme happiness that visits a quieted mind — even thirty calm seconds carry the signature.
verses.background: The mind has been brought back again and again. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as what follows for the one who keeps re-taming it, once the restless quality of passion (rajas) is spent: the joy of absorption, which arrives of itself.
verses.hook: What does the meditator experience once the mind is calm and passions quiet?

refs.note: One who attains divine love sees, hears, speaks of and thinks only of the Beloved, the absorption that brings the supreme bliss.

views.text: 'Become Brahman' means liberated while living, with the certainty that Brahman is all; the rajas that is stilled covers defects like delusion.
'For' gives the reason: the self is by nature supreme bliss. 'Become Brahman' means steady in one's own essential nature as the self.
The grammar is pointed: bliss is the agent that comes, and the yogi is its object; once the mind rests in the Self, bliss arrives on its own.
As the mind is withdrawn from sense objects and fixed on God, passions subside and it runs to Him naturally. Growing inner bliss is the sign that one is truly progressing.

verses.devanagari:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी विगतकल्मषः ।
सुखेन ब्रह्मसंस्पर्शमत्यन्तं सुखमश्नुते॥
verses.transliteration:
yuñjannevaṃ sadātmānaṃ yogī vigatakalmaṣaḥ
sukhena brahmasaṃsparśamatyantaṃ sukhamaśnute
verses.essence: Thus ever harnessing the self, the yogi freed from stain easily enjoys the boundless bliss of contact with Brahman.
verses.translation: The Yogi, always engaging the mind thus (in the practice of Yoga), freed from sins, easily enjoys the Infinite Bliss of contact with Brahman (the Eternal).

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while doing)

anvaya.parts: विगत (gone away) + कल्मष (stain): one whose stains have gone

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, instrumental singular, used as adverb (with ease)

anvaya.parts: ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) + संस्पर्श (contact): the bliss that is contact with Brahman

verses.explanation: Two words elevate this beyond 6.27: sukhena, *easily* — the struggle phase ends; practice becomes the path of least resistance — and brahma-saṁsparśa, the *touch* of Brahman. Not inference, not belief: contact, the most intimate word the body knows, borrowed for the soul's encounter with the Absolute.
verses.connection: Completes the inner arc: the discipline of 6.24–26 matured into effortless communion.
verses.reflection: Touch the boundless once today — through breath, prayer, or silence — and let it perfume the hours after.
verses.background: Follows the supreme bliss of 6.27. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as the point where the yogi's purpose is fulfilled, "he has done what was to be done," and reads the touch of Brahman (the Absolute) as direct realization, freedom while living.
verses.hook: What happiness comes to a yogi who keeps practising this way?

refs.note: Divides happiness into tamasic, rajasic, sattvic and the one beyond the modes, which rests in God; the verse speaks of this highest kind.

views.text: The sinless yogi, freed from the obstacles to Yoga, easily attains bliss beyond all limits, in touch with supreme Brahman; the result of this Yoga is realizing identity with Brahman, which ends all worldly existence.
Brahman here means the self: the bliss is the joy of experiencing it, gained easily, without strain. The next verses lay out four degrees of mature yoga.
'Easily' is the point: by settling the mind in the Self the yogi reaches Brahman, not by some difficult yoga.
'Contact with Brahman' is direct realization that ends ignorance; that is the supreme bliss, and the yogi becomes liberated while living.

Happiness comes in four kinds: from intoxication, from the senses, from virtue and self-knowledge, and the divine bliss beyond the modes. The yogi united with God reaches this last, infinite happiness.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वभूतस्थमात्मानं सर्वभूतानि चात्मनि ।
ईक्षते योगयुक्तात्मा सर्वत्र समदर्शनः॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvabhūtasthamātmānaṃ sarvabhūtāni cātmani
īkṣate yogayuktātmā sarvatra samadarśanaḥ
verses.essence: One harnessed in yoga, seeing the same everywhere, sees the Self present in all beings and all beings in the Self.
verses.translation: With the mind harmonised by Yoga he sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he sees the same everywhere.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being) + स्थ (standing in): that which abides in all beings
सर्व (all) + भूत (being): all beings

anvaya.meaning: one whose self is joined in yoga
anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + युक्त (joined) + आत्मन् (self): one whose self is united through yoga
सम (same, equal) + दर्शन (seeing): one whose seeing is equal

verses.explanation: The eyes open, and the meditation's fruit turns out to be a way of seeing the world: one Self threaded through every being, every being held within the one Self — both directions at once, in words close to the Īśa Upaniṣad's sixth verse. Sama-darśana returns from 5.18, now not as ethics practiced but as perception delivered. Hours on the seat are validated not by visions but by whether the gaze, rising, finds the same one everywhere: sarvatra sama-darśanaḥ — the cushion's diploma is issued in the street.
verses.connection: The pivot outward: 6.28's inner touch becomes 6.29–32's universal vision.
verses.reflection: Look at one stranger today and silently note: the same Self there as here. Equal vision, one rep.
verses.background: Śaṅkara introduces this verse as the result of yoga that is the realization of oneness with Brahman (the Absolute), the cause of the end of worldly existence. After the inner practice of 6.24–28, Krishna turns to how such a yogi sees all that lives.
verses.hook: How does a yogi in harmony see the self and all beings?

refs.note: As a fire in one place spreads light everywhere, the Supreme pervades and sustains the whole world through His energies.

views.text: Sameness means knowing the identity of the Self and Brahman in everything, from the creator Brahmā down to a clump of grass, seen as unified in one's own Self.
Freed from the body, all selves are alike as knowledge; differences belong to the body only. So the yogi sees himself in all beings by likeness: to see one self truly is to see them all.
The Self is seen entering all beings as the perceiver in them, and all beings are gathered into the Self as what it knows; from this comes the power to see equally.
Like candies in many shapes all made of sugar, everything is made of God's energies. Perfected yogis see everything in its connection with God.

verses.devanagari:
यो मां पश्यति सर्वत्र सर्वं च मयि पश्यति ।
तस्याहं न प्रणश्यामि स च मे न प्रणश्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
yo māṃ paśyati sarvatra sarvaṃ ca mayi paśyati
tasyāhaṃ na praṇaśyāmi sa ca me na praṇaśyati
verses.essence: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me — I am never lost to that one, nor is that one ever lost to me.
verses.translation: He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me, he never becomes separated from Me, nor do I become separated from him.
verses.explanation: The chapter's most tender promise, and it is mutual: na praṇaśyāmi — I am not lost to him, nor is he lost to me. Here the impersonal vision of 6.29 gains a face and a vow. Whoever has learned to find Krishna in all things, and all things in him, can no longer lose him in any circumstance; and such a seer is held, never dropped, never out of sight. Two gazes, permanently locked: the all-pervading turns out to be Someone, and that Someone promises not to vanish.
verses.connection: Personalizes 6.29: the universal Self acquires a face, and the seeing becomes a relationship.
verses.reflection: Hold the promise close in a lonely hour: see Him everywhere, and you are never lost to Him.
verses.background: Krishna has just described the yogi who sees the Self in all beings. Śaṅkara introduces this verse as the fruit of that realization of unity; Krishna now speaks in the first person, as "me."
verses.hook: How can you stay connected to God at every moment?

refs.note: When loss comes in the world, do not grieve over it, having offered oneself to God; see His hand in it.

views.text: The seer of unity is never lost to the Lord because they are identical: one's own Self is surely dear, and it is the Lord himself who sees the unity in all.
The freed self, seeing its likeness to the Lord, never loses sight of Him; and the Lord, seeing Himself, always has that yogi in view because of the likeness.
'Lost' means failing to appear: whoever misses the all-pervading consciousness has lost it, since nothing shines without it; whoever sees objects resting in it is never lost to it.
'Not lost' means the Lord becomes directly visible and looks on that devotee with a glance of grace, favouring him.
To lose God is to let the mind wander from Him. Seeing God in everyone and every event, even those who hurt us and losses we grieve, keeps the mind united with Him until we are never lost to Him.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वभूतस्थितं यो मां भजत्येकत्वमास्थितः ।
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि स योगी मयि वर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvabhūtasthitaṃ yo māṃ bhajatyekatvamāsthitaḥ
sarvathā vartamāno'pi sa yogī mayi vartate
verses.essence: The yogi who, established in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all beings — that one abides in me, whatever the manner of living.
verses.translation: He who, being established in unity, worships Me Who dwells in all beings, that Yogi abides in Me, whatever may be his mode of living.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being) + स्थित (abiding): the one abiding in all beings

verses.explanation: Sarvathā vartamāno 'pi — however such a one happens to be living: in a forest or a market, in robes or armor. Once worship has become the perception of the One in all, lifestyle ceases to be the measure; the address is fixed — mayi vartate, dwelling in me — regardless of the outer route.
verses.connection: Extends 6.30's mutual sight into mutual residence, dissolving the monk-versus-householder question.
verses.reflection: Worship through your situation today, whatever it is — the one-in-all accepts every mode of living.
verses.background: Śrīdhara introduces this verse against a lingering worry: is such a knower still bound to serve ritual rules? Krishna answers right after promising, in 6.30, that he and the one who sees him everywhere are never lost to each other.
verses.hook: Can someone abide in God whatever their way of life?

refs.note: Tells of Śukadeva, so absorbed in God as he left home that he did not notice the world; even the trees answered his father's call.

views.text: The second line states the result of full realization: liberation. Whatever condition he is in, he exists in the supreme state and is ever free; nothing obstructs his release.
Even after coming out of meditation, however he lives, such a yogi sees only the Lord whenever he looks at his own self or at other beings.
Such a knower is no longer a servant of ritual injunctions: even living without rites he abides in the Lord and is released, never falling.
Vision rises in stages: seeing everyone as a body, as a soul, God seated within everyone, and finally God alone. This verse speaks of perfected yogis at the two highest stages.

verses.devanagari:
आत्मौपम्येन सर्वत्र समं पश्यति योऽर्जुन ।
सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं स योगी परमो मतः॥
verses.transliteration:
ātmaupamyena sarvatra samaṃ paśyati yo'rjuna
sukhaṃ vā yadi vā duḥkhaṃ sa yogī paramo mataḥ
verses.essence: One who, by the analogy of the self, sees the same everywhere — in joy or in sorrow — is deemed the highest yogi, Arjuna.
verses.translation: He who, through the likeness of the Self, O Arjuna, sees equality everywhere, be it pleasure or pain, he is regarded as the highest Yogi.

anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (oneself) + औपम्य (comparison): judging by the standard of oneself
