anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular (used as adverb)
past participle, masculine, nominative singular (is regarded)

verses.explanation: The vision's ethical edge: ātmaupamya, taking oneself as the measure — their pain weighed on the scale of my pain, their joy on the scale of mine. The golden rule, but grounded in metaphysics rather than prudence: the other's suffering matters like mine because, at the depth just seen, the other *is* mine. The one who sees this way is crowned paramaḥ — deemed the highest yogi of all.
verses.connection: Caps the vision-section: the summit of meditation is measured, finally, in compassion.
verses.reflection: Use your own pain as the translator today: feel one person's joy or sorrow as if it were yours.
verses.background: The last verse of Krishna's long teaching before Arjuna breaks in. Śrīdhara presents it as naming, among the yogis who worship Krishna in this way, the one who is best; Krishna addresses Arjuna by name.
verses.hook: Who is the highest yogi?

views.text: As happiness is dear to me and sorrow unwelcome, so it is for every creature; seeing this, he harms no one. The non-injurious one, steady in full knowledge, is the best of yogis.

Not a call to feel others' joys and sorrows as one's own: the yogi sees that his self is untouched by pleasures and pains such as a son's birth or death, and that every other self is equally untouched.
Among those who worship the Lord, the best is the one compassionate to all beings, who wishes happiness for everyone and sorrow for none.
As we feel harm to any limb as harm to ourselves, yogis who see God in all beings feel others' joys and sorrows as their own and always work for everyone's eternal good.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
योऽयं योगस्त्वया प्रोक्तः साम्येन मधुसूदन ।
एतस्याहं न पश्यामि चञ्चलत्वात्स्थितिं स्थिराम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yo'yaṃ yogastvayā proktaḥ sāmyena madhusūdana
etasyāhaṃ na paśyāmi cañcalatvātsthitiṃ sthirām
verses.essence: Arjuna says: this yoga of evenness you have taught, Madhusudana — because of restlessness, I do not see how it can stand firm.
verses.translation: This Yoga of equanimity taught by Thee, O Krishna, I do not see its steady continuance, because of the restlessness (of the mind).

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by way of)

anvaya.parts: मधु (the demon Madhu) + सूदन (slayer): the slayer of Madhu

verses.explanation: After thirty-two verses of luminous instruction, the student raises his hand with the objection every meditator owns: it sounds beautiful, but my mind won't hold it. Arjuna's honesty rescues the chapter from idealism — the lamp may be windless in theory; his is guttering.
verses.connection: The voice of every practitioner interrupting 6.29–32's heights with the floor's-eye view.
verses.reflection: Admit your restlessness honestly, as Arjuna did — diagnosis spoken aloud is half the discipline.
verses.background: Arjuna speaks for the first time in the chapter, after a long unbroken teaching. Śaṅkara says he finds this yoga hard to attain and wants to hear a sure means to it. "This yoga" refers back to the method taught from 6.10 onward.
verses.hook: Can anyone really keep this equanimity when the mind is so restless?

views.text: Arjuna cannot conceive how the Yoga taught as sameness could continue steadily and undisturbed, given the well-known unsteadiness of the mind.
The 'evenness' taught is seeing all selves, gods and men alike, as equal in being knowledge, and seeing them as like the Supreme in being free of karma; Arjuna doubts a fickle mind can hold this.
Evenness means the mind free of both sinking into dullness and scattering, resting only in the form of the Self; Arjuna doubts it can last for long.
Arjuna frankly finds the yoga just described impractical, because subduing the senses, giving up desires, fixing the mind on God and equal vision all depend on controlling the restless mind.

verses.devanagari:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद् दृढम् ।
तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्॥
verses.transliteration:
cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavad dṛḍham
tasyāhaṃ nigrahaṃ manye vāyoriva suduṣkaram
verses.essence: For the mind is restless, Krishna — turbulent, strong, obstinate. To restrain it, I think, is as hard as restraining the wind.
verses.translation: The mind verily is restless, turbulent, strong and unyielding, O Krishna: I deem it as difficult to control it as to control the wind.

anvaya.parts: सु (very) + दुष्कर (hard to do): extremely hard to accomplish

verses.explanation: Four adjectives, each worse than the last: restless, then pramāthi — churning, actively agitating its owner — then strong, then dṛḍham, set in its ways. The simile is a warrior's: he has bent bows and broken armies, but the wind one cannot grip. The complaint is ancient and not a day stale.
verses.connection: Spells out the restlessness Arjuna gave in 6.33 as his reason, ending with the wind; Krishna's reply in 6.35 begins by conceding it.
verses.reflection: Watch the mind for one minute and respect the opponent: turbulent, strong, obstinate — and trainable.
verses.background: Arjuna continues his objection. Śrīdhara says this verse spells out the restlessness of mind he gave as his reason in 6.33, listing its traits one by one before closing with an image from nature.
verses.hook: Why does controlling the mind feel as hard as holding the wind?

views.text: Explains 'Krishna' from the root kṛṣ, to uproot: he uproots his devotees' sins. The mind torments body and senses and is gripped like the tantu-nāga; Arjuna thinks it harder to control than the wind.
The mind wanders even from what it has long practised; fixing it on the self, its very opposite, is like holding back a gale with a flimsy fan. Arjuna is really asking for the means.
The methods just taught have shown Brahman almost as if perceived, yet the mind's restlessness keeps it far away; 'churning' means the mind ruins both seen and unseen goals.

Arjuna speaks for all of us: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate. By calling the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the one who attracts even great yogis' minds, he hints that Kṛṣṇa should draw his mind too.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
असंशयं महाबाहो मनो दुर्निग्रहं चलम् ।
अभ्यासेन तु कौन्तेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
asaṃśayaṃ mahābāho mano durnigrahaṃ calam
abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate
verses.essence: Doubtless, mighty-armed one, the mind is hard to restrain and restless. But by practice, Kaunteya, and by dispassion, it is held.
verses.translation: Undoubtedly, O mighty-armed Arjuna, the mind is difficult to control and restless; but by practice and by dispassion it may be restrained.

anvaya.parts: अ (without) + संशय (doubt): without doubt
महा (great) + बाहु (arm): one whose arms are mighty
दुस् (hard) + निग्रह (restraint): hard to hold down

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done to it)

verses.explanation: First, the concession — asaṁśayam, no argument: you are right about the wind. Then the two-word cure that all later yoga inherits: abhyāsa, repetition that wears a channel, and vairāgya, the cooling of the cravings that supply the wind in the first place; Patañjali's Yoga-sūtra (1.12) names the same pair. Effort on one side, release on the other — held between them, the mind is caught: gṛhyate.
verses.connection: Answers 6.34 by first agreeing the mind is restless and hard to hold, then naming the two means that tame it: practice and dispassion.
verses.reflection: Use both reins today: practice when fresh, dispassion when tempted — abhyasa and vairagya together.
verses.background: Krishna answers Arjuna's objection, and Śaṅkara's lead-in has him agree first: 'This is just as you say.' He calls Arjuna "mighty-armed," which Mukundananda hears as a reminder that the warrior who has beaten great fighters can master his own mind.
verses.hook: Can a restless mind really be brought under control?

refs.note: Patañjali says the mind's fluctuations are stilled by practice and detachment, the same two means named in this verse.

views.text: Practice is the repetition of one idea on a chosen object; dispassion is the absence of hankering for any enjoyment, seen or unseen, born of seeing its defects.

Practice here is repeated contemplation of the self's auspicious qualities, such as eternity, self-luminosity and bliss, which makes the mind turn toward the self; dispassion comes from seeing the flaws in everything else.
The two remedies cover the mind's two faults: practice stops its sinking into dullness, dispassion stops its scattering, and the stilled mind then takes the form of the Supreme.
Kṛṣṇa admits the mind is hard to control but says it can be done. Detachment takes the mind off the world and practice brings it to rest on God, as skill grows with repetition.

verses.devanagari:
असंयतात्मना योगो दुष्प्राप इति मे मतिः ।
वश्यात्मना तु यतता शक्योऽवाप्तुमुपायतः॥
verses.transliteration:
asaṃyatātmanā yogo duṣprāpa iti me matiḥ
vaśyātmanā tu yatatā śakyo'vāptumupāyataḥ
verses.essence: For one of unrestrained self, yoga is hard to attain — this is my view. But for the self-governed who strives, it can be won by right means.
verses.translation: I think Yoga is hard to be attained by one of uncontrolled self, but the self-controlled and striving one can attain to it by the (proper) means.

anvaya.base: असंयतात्मन् · one whose mind is uncontrolled
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + संयत (restrained) + आत्मन् (self, mind): one whose mind is not restrained
दुस् (hard) + प्राप (to be reached): hard to reach

anvaya.base: वश्यात्मन् · one whose mind is mastered
anvaya.parts: वश्य (controlled) + आत्मन् (self, mind): one whose mind is under control

verses.explanation: Honest pricing: duṣprāpa, genuinely hard — the Gita does not discount the difficulty to make a sale. But the hardness is conditional, not absolute, and the final word carries the hope: upāyataḥ, by method. What will cannot storm, technique can win; the gate is locked, and there is a key.
verses.connection: Seals the exchange of 6.33–35: difficulty conceded, impossibility denied.
verses.reflection: Stop demanding self-mastery in one leap; strive by the right means today and call that success.
verses.background: Śaṅkara's lead-in, "By him, however, who has not controlled his mind—", runs straight into this verse, so it completes Krishna's reply to Arjuna's objection. It is his last word on taming the mind before Arjuna asks something new.
verses.hook: Who can succeed in yoga, and who will find it very hard?

views.text: Yoga is hard for one whose mind is not mastered through practice and detachment, yet attainable by one who strives repeatedly by the means taught. This raises the worry that a yogi dying before full Illumination may be ruined.

The mind is subdued through the karma-yoga taught earlier, which is worship of the Lord and contains knowledge; that is the 'means'. This leads Arjuna back to the promise of 2.40 that no effort is lost.
'Uncontrolled' means lacking desirelessness; 'one who strives' means one who practises; the 'means' are those laid down in the Siddhānta and other scriptures.
Those who have not reined in the mind through practice and detachment struggle in yoga, while those who have, by persistent effort, succeed through the process already described.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
अयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः ।
अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
ayatiḥ śraddhayopeto yogāccalitamānasaḥ
aprāpya yogasaṃsiddhiṃ kāṃ gatiṃ kṛṣṇa gacchati
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: one who has faith but insufficient effort, whose mind falls from yoga before reaching perfection — what way does such a one go, Krishna?
verses.translation: He who is unable to control himself though he has the faith, and whose mind wanders away from Yoga, what end does he, having failed to attain perfection in Yoga, meet, O Krishna?

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + यति (effort): one who does not strive
चलित (moved away) + मानस (mind): one whose mind has moved away
योग (yoga) + संसिद्धि (full success): the perfection of yoga

verses.explanation: The bravest question in the chapter: what about the one who tried and failed? Faith intact, effort insufficient, journey unfinished — death arrives mid-path. Arjuna is not asking abstractly; a man about to attempt the hardest discipline wants to know the cost of falling short.
verses.connection: Opens the great consolation passage (6.37–45): the fate of the sincere but incomplete.
verses.reflection: Bring your honest fear of failing the path into the open — the question itself is held kindly.
verses.background: Arjuna speaks again. Krishna has just said yoga is won by the self-controlled who strive; Arjuna now asks about one who sets out sincerely but falls short. Śaṅkara frames the fear: such a person gives up the rewards of this world and the next, then dies before illumination.
verses.hook: What becomes of a person of faith who falls short in yoga?

views.text: Faith here is belief in God and the other world; the person lacks effort in yoga, and at death his mind strays from it, his memory lost.
He entered yoga sincerely, with faith and not as pretence, but his practice was slack and his dispassion weak, so he did not reach knowledge.

The journey begins with faith, which may come from past impressions, saintly company or setbacks. If such seekers grow lax, the restless mind stops them finishing in this life, and Arjuna asks their fate.

verses.devanagari:
कच्चिन्नोभयविभ्रष्टश्छिन्नाभ्रमिव नश्यति ।
अप्रतिष्ठो महाबाहो विमूढो ब्रह्मणः पथि॥
verses.transliteration:
kaccinnobhayavibhraṣṭaśchinnābhramiva naśyati
apratiṣṭho mahābāho vimūḍho brahmaṇaḥ pathi
verses.essence: Fallen from both, does he not perish like a riven cloud — without support, bewildered on the path to Brahman?
verses.translation: Fallen from both, does he not perish like a rent cloud, supportless, O mighty-armed one, deluded on the path of Brahman?

anvaya.parts: उभय (both) + विभ्रष्ट (fallen away): one fallen from both
छिन्न (torn off) + अभ्र (cloud): a cloud torn away
अ (without) + प्रतिष्ठा (footing): one with no footing
महा (great) + बाहु (arm): one whose arms are mighty

verses.explanation: The fear given its full image: ubhaya-vibhraṣṭa, fallen from both worlds — having renounced the worldly race, yet missing the spiritual finish — like a small cloud torn from its bank, dissolving in empty sky, belonging nowhere. It is the secret terror of everyone who has ever left a safe shore for an uncertain crossing.
verses.connection: Intensifies 6.37: the double loss feared by all who stake ordinary success on extraordinary hope.
verses.reflection: When you feel between two worlds — committed to neither — remember the question was asked for you.
verses.background: Arjuna presses his question, and Śrīdhara says this verse explains its intent. Having offered his works to God and left rites undone, the seeker forgoes heaven; having not completed yoga, he misses liberation. Arjuna's image for that loss comes from the monsoon sky.
verses.text_note: The translation of this verse was missing in the source dataset; it is taken from the Sivananda text in the gita/gita dataset.
verses.hook: Is a seeker who fails at yoga left with neither world nor God?

views.text: Ritual cannot support him, since he acted without wanting its fruits, and he has lost his way on the newly begun path to Brahman: does he fall from both heaven and liberation?
He gets no heaven, since his acts were offered to God or left undone, and no liberation, since yoga was unfinished; like a cloud broken from one mass that melts away before reaching another.
Arjun fears that one who gave up worldly aims for God and then failed ends up like a stray cloud, with neither material gain nor spiritual attainment.

verses.devanagari:
एतन्मे संशयं कृष्ण छेत्तुमर्हस्यशेषतः ।
त्वदन्यः संशयस्यास्य छेत्ता न ह्युपपद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
etanme saṃśayaṃ kṛṣṇa chettumarhasyaśeṣataḥ
tvadanyaḥ saṃśayasyāsya chettā na hyupapadyate
verses.essence: This doubt of mine, Krishna, please dispel without remainder — for none but you can be the destroyer of this doubt.
verses.translation: This doubt of mine, O Krishna, do Thou dispel completely; because it is not possible for any but Thee to dispel this doubt.

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, accusative singular (stands for masculine एनम्, with संशयम्)
noun, masculine, nominative singular (agent: the one who does)

verses.explanation: Arjuna asks for surgery, not reassurance: chettum, cut it — aśeṣataḥ, leaving no root to regrow. And he names why he asks here: on the question of what happens to the failed soul, only the one who oversees souls can answer. Some doubts outrank every human authority.
verses.connection: Hands 6.37–38's fear to the only court competent to rule on it.
verses.reflection: Take your unresolvable doubt to the highest court you know today, and actually wait for the answer.
verses.background: Arjuna ends the question of 6.37–39 by appealing to Krishna personally. Śaṅkara glosses the "none other" as no one else, whether sage or god, so that Krishna himself must remove the doubt.
verses.hook: Why does Arjuna turn to Krishna alone to settle his doubt?

views.text: No one other than Krishna, be he a sage or a god, can destroy this doubt, so Krishna himself must remove it totally.
Only Krishna can remove this doubt because he alone perceives all things directly and at once.
The fallen yogi's faith is not lost, and faith is what counts: even perfect knowledge, spoiled by the mind's caprice, perishes like cotton in fire.
Scholars hold only theoretical knowledge and even realized saints know in limited measure; only the all-knowing God can remove every doubt, as the sun removes darkness.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
पार्थ नैवेह नामुत्र विनाशस्तस्य विद्यते ।
न हि कल्याणकृत्कश्चिद् दुर्गतिं तात गच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
pārtha naiveha nāmutra vināśastasya vidyate
na hi kalyāṇakṛtkaścid durgatiṃ tāta gacchati
verses.essence: Partha, neither here nor hereafter is there destruction for him. No one who does good, dear friend, ever comes to grief.
verses.translation: O Arjuna, neither in this world, nor in the next world is there destruction for him; none, verily, who does good, O My son, ever comes to grief.

anvaya.parts: कल्याण (good, auspicious) + कृत् (doer): one who does good
दुस् (bad) + गति (going, destination): a bad destination

verses.explanation: The answer opens with the rarest address Krishna uses: tāta — dear child, a father's word to a disciple. Then the universal amnesty: na hi kalyāṇa-kṛt kaścid durgatiṁ gacchati — no one who does good ever travels to a bad end, not in this world, not beyond. In this cosmos, sincere effort is a deposit that cannot be confiscated: the path keeps every deposit, honors every partial effort, and fears no incomplete life. The universe keeps honest books.
verses.connection: The thunderclap of consolation answering 6.38's torn cloud: nothing offered upward is lost.
verses.reflection: Engrave the amnesty somewhere visible: no one who does good ever comes to a bad end.
verses.background: Krishna replies to the fear of the seeker who falls short. Śrīdhara says the answer runs four and a half verses, counts the seeker a doer of good because he entered yoga with faith, and calls the address tāta ("dear one") a tender, everyday word.
verses.hook: What becomes of someone who sincerely tries but falls short on the spiritual path?

views.text: Ruin means a birth lower than the previous one, which does not happen to him. 'Tāta' is explained: the father extends himself through the son, so a son, and a disciple, is called tāta.
No loss in either sense: neither failure to gain what he sought, nor the harm that comes from faults in performing works. No one practising this auspicious yoga meets an evil end.
He keeps his faith, and seeking the Lord is an act that does not perish, unlike the fruits of rites such as the Agniṣṭoma.
Calling Arjun 'dear son', Krishna shows a father's affection: God protects those who walk his path, in this life and the next, which is a great assurance to every seeker.

verses.devanagari:
प्राप्य पुण्यकृतां लोकानुषित्वा शाश्वतीः समाः ।
शुचीनां श्रीमतां गेहे योगभ्रष्टोऽभिजायते॥
verses.transliteration:
prāpya puṇyakṛtāṃ lokānuṣitvā śāśvatīḥ samāḥ
śucīnāṃ śrīmatāṃ gehe yogabhraṣṭo'bhijāyate
verses.essence: Having reached the worlds of the righteous and dwelt there for long years, the one fallen from yoga is born in the home of the pure and prosperous.
verses.translation: Having attained to the worlds of the righteous and having dwelt there for everlasting years, he who fell from Yoga is born in a house of the pure and wealthy.

anvaya.parts: पुण्य (merit) + कृत् (doer): those who do meritorious deeds

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, accusative plural (for how long)

anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + भ्रष्ट (fallen): one who has fallen from yoga

verses.explanation: The itinerary of the unfinished: first rest — long ages in luminous worlds, the effort honored — then re-entry, and not at random: a household clean in conduct and free of want, soil chosen for the seed. The interrupted journey resumes with better provisions than it had.
verses.connection: Begins detailing 6.40's promise: failure rerouted, never erased.
verses.reflection: Trust that your past efforts are banked — you may be living, right now, off a forgotten deposit.
verses.background: Krishna has promised that the one fallen from yoga is not destroyed, which leaves the question Śaṅkara puts before this verse: 'But what happens to him?' Here Krishna begins to trace that person's path after death.
verses.hook: Where is the unsuccessful yogi born after death?

views.text: The one fallen from yoga is, from the context, a monk who renounced works but did not reach perfection; the 'pure' are householders who act by scriptural rule.
He strayed from yoga out of desire for enjoyments, so by yoga's own power he receives them, staying in those worlds until the desire is spent; then he is born in a family fit to practise yoga.
'Everlasting years' means only a very long time, not literally eternal; the righteous are those who live truthfully and act by the scriptures.
A yogi falls through desire for enjoyment, so God may first let him taste heavenly pleasures and learn their futility, then grant birth in a pious or wealthy home where practice can continue.

verses.devanagari:
अथवा योगिनामेव कुले भवति धीमताम् ।
एतद्धि दुर्लभतरं लोके जन्म यदीदृशम्॥
verses.transliteration:
athavā yogināmeva kule bhavati dhīmatām
etaddhi durlabhataraṃ loke janma yadīdṛśam
verses.essence: Or one is born into a family of wise yogis themselves — such a birth as this is exceedingly rare in the world.
verses.translation: Or he is born in a family of even the wise Yogis; verily a birth like this is very difficult to obtain in this world.
verses.explanation: The express route for the further-along: birth straight into a lineage of practitioners, where the path is the family business and the atmosphere itself instructs. Durlabhataram — rarer still, harder to come by than the prosperous birth of 6.41: the tradition prized being born among the wise above being born among the wealthy.
verses.connection: The second landing-site after 6.41, graded to how far the traveler had come.
verses.reflection: If wisdom feels strangely native to you, honor the rarity — and do not waste the head start.
verses.background: Krishna is still answering Arjuna's fear about the yogi who falls short in this life. Having placed one kind of fallen yogi in a pure and prosperous home, he now names the other landing. Śrīdhara introduces it as the case of one who had practised long before falling, and so is born among wise yogis.
verses.hook: What rarer birth may await a yogi who had advanced far?

views.text: These are families of wise but poor yogis, as distinct from the prosperous of the previous verse; such a birth is harder to obtain.
This birth comes to one who strayed at an advanced stage: he is born among accomplished yogins able to teach yoga. Both births are rare, yet yoga's power secures them.
This birth is harder to get, and better, because a rich household is full of obstacles.
Yogis who had already gained dispassion skip the heavenly detour and are born to spiritually evolved parents, a rare fortune because divine wisdom is taught from childhood.

verses.devanagari:
तत्र तं बुद्धिसंयोगं लभते पौर्वदेहिकम् ।
यतते च ततो भूयः संसिद्धौ कुरुनन्दन॥
verses.transliteration:
tatra taṃ buddhisaṃyogaṃ labhate paurvadehikam
yatate ca tato bhūyaḥ saṃsiddhau kurunandana
verses.essence: There one regains the union of understanding earned in the former body, and strives onward again toward perfection, Kurunandana.
verses.translation: Thee he comes in touch with the knowledge acquired in his former body and strives more than before for perfection, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: बुद्धि (understanding) + संयोग (union, connection): connection with the understanding

anvaya.base: पौर्वदेहिक · belonging to the previous body
anvaya.parts: पूर्व (former) + देह (body), with the -इक ending: belonging to the former body

anvaya.base: कुरुनन्दन · Arjuna, delight of the Kurus
anvaya.parts: कुरु (the Kuru line) + नन्दन (joy, son): the joy of the Kurus

verses.explanation: The mechanics of continuity: paurva-dehikam, the prior body's cultivated understanding, restored like a file reopened. Nothing learned in the inner life had evaporated; it waited. Hence the unexplainable affinities of childhood — the pull toward silence, scripture, or the sacred that arrives before any teaching could have planted it.
verses.connection: Explains how 6.41–42's new births resume rather than restart the journey.
verses.reflection: Notice what draws you even against convenience — previous practice is pulling. Let it.
verses.background: Arjuna has just heard of the two homes, prosperous or yogic, into which the fallen yogi is reborn. The natural next question is what happens there. Śrīdhara opens the verse with exactly that: "what then?" Krishna now tells what the newborn seeker finds waiting in that life.
verses.hook: Does spiritual progress from a past life carry over into the next?

views.text: Born into a family of yogis, he regains the wisdom acquired in his previous body and strives for perfection more intensely than that earlier tendency.
Like someone waking from sleep, he picks up exactly where he left off and strives so as not to be beaten again by obstacles.
Past practice survives as subtle impressions in the subconscious; reawakened in the new birth, they push the seeker to strive harder than before.
God, seated within, keeps account of every past spiritual asset and reawakens it at the right time, so the yogi resumes the journey like a traveller waking at a wayside inn.

verses.devanagari:
पूर्वाभ्यासेन तेनैव ह्रियते ह्यवशोऽपि सः ।
जिज्ञासुरपि योगस्य शब्दब्रह्मातिवर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
pūrvābhyāsena tenaiva hriyate hyavaśo'pi saḥ
jijñāsurapi yogasya śabdabrahmātivartate
verses.essence: By that very former practice one is carried onward, even despite oneself. Even the mere inquirer into yoga passes beyond the Veda's word.
verses.translation: By that very former practice he is borne on in spite of himself. Even he who merely wishes to know Yoga goes beyond the Brahmic word.

anvaya.parts: पूर्व (former) + अभ्यास (practice): practice done before

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done to him)

anvaya.base: अवश · not under one's own control
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + वश (control): not by one's own will

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, nominative singular (desire form: wanting to know)

anvaya.parts: शब्द (word, sound) + ब्रह्मन् (Brahman): Brahman in the form of words

verses.explanation: Hriyate avaśo 'pi — carried, even unwilling: old practice becomes a current under the boat, momentum that no longer requires the rower's consent. And a stunning aside: even the jijñāsu, the one who has merely begun *asking* about yoga, already outruns śabda-brahma, religion-as-formula. The question outranks the recitation.
verses.connection: Completes the consolation's logic: practice compounds across lives, and even curiosity counts.
verses.reflection: Honor the seeker's restlessness in you; even the wish to know already outruns ritual.
verses.background: Krishna has said the reborn yogi regains his earlier understanding and strives again. Śaṅkara has just asked how that old wisdom comes back to him, and this verse gives the reason. It then widens the reassurance from the long-practised yogi to someone who has only begun to ask what yoga is.
verses.hook: Why do some people feel pulled toward God almost against their will?

views.text: The habit of yoga can be held back for a while by a stronger wrong deed, but it is never destroyed and resumes once that is spent; 'word-Brahman' means the results of Vedic ritual.
'Word-Brahman' here is matter (prakṛti), which takes the forms named by words like gods, men, earth and heaven; the seeker passes beyond it to the self made of knowledge and bliss.
Passing beyond the 'word' means he no longer takes up what only strengthens sacred sound, such as hymn recitation; this comes from his mere desire to know yoga.
Devotional impressions once sown cannot be erased; they become a call of God strong enough to make princes renounce comfort and rise above rituals aimed at material gain.

verses.devanagari:
प्रयत्नाद्यतमानस्तु योगी संशुद्धकिल्बिषः ।
अनेकजन्मसंसिद्धस्ततो याति परां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
prayatnādyatamānastu yogī saṃśuddhakilbiṣaḥ
anekajanmasaṃsiddhastato yāti parāṃ gatim
verses.essence: But the yogi striving with effort, cleansed of stain, perfected through many births, then reaches the supreme goal.
verses.translation: But the Yogi who strives with assiduity, purified of sins and perfected gradually through many births, reaches the highest goal.

anvaya.parts: संशुद्ध (fully cleansed) + किल्बिष (sin, stain): one whose sins are washed away
अनेक (many) + जन्मन् (birth) + संसिद्ध (perfected): perfected through many births

verses.explanation: The honest timescale: aneka-janma-saṁsiddhaḥ — perfected across many births. The path may be longer than a lifetime, and the Gita declines to pretend otherwise; what it removes is not the length but the fear of the length. Every step banks; no birth starts from zero; the arrival, however delayed, is arithmetic.
verses.connection: Seals 6.37–44: the failed yogi's question answered with a multi-life guarantee.
verses.reflection: Take the long view of your striving tonight: many lives of polishing, then the goal. No panic.
verses.background: If even a hesitant beginner is carried past the rituals of the Veda, Śrīdhara reasons, how much more the yogi who keeps pressing on. Krishna now states that stronger case, closing his long answer to Arjuna's question (6.37–39) about the seeker who fails.
verses.hook: How does a yogi finally reach the supreme goal?

views.text: Impressions are gathered little by little over many births; perfected by their total, the yogi gains full illumination and so reaches the highest goal.
Success should not be credited to the one life just ended: it was practised through many lifetimes, and at the body's end he attains identity with Vāsudeva.
An argument from the lesser case: if even a yogi of slack effort reaches the supreme goal, what need to say it of one who strives harder and harder?
Past practice is a favourable wind; the yogi now raises the sail of sincere, harder effort. What looks like success in one life is the fruit of many lives' practice.

verses.devanagari:
तपस्विभ्योऽधिको योगी ज्ञानिभ्योऽपि मतोऽधिकः ।
कर्मिभ्यश्चाधिको योगी तस्माद्योगी भवार्जुन॥
verses.transliteration:
tapasvibhyo'dhiko yogī jñānibhyo'pi mato'dhikaḥ
karmibhyaścādhiko yogī tasmādyogī bhavārjuna
verses.essence: The yogi is greater than ascetics, deemed greater even than the knowers, and greater than the doers of works. Therefore be a yogi, Arjuna.
verses.translation: The Yogi is thought to be superior to the ascetics and even superior to men of knowledge (obtained through the study of scriptures); he is also superior to men of action; therefore be thou a Yogi, O Arjuna.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (is regarded)

verses.explanation: Three honored vocations measured and ranked below one: above the tapasvī who masters the body, the jñānī of the texts, the karmī of the rites stands the yogi — the one in whom discipline, knowledge and action have fused into inward union. Then the chapter's whole teaching compressed into three words of direct address: tasmād yogī bhava.
verses.connection: Turns the answer of 6.40-45 into a command: since no effort in yoga is lost, the yogi outranks ascetic, scholar and ritualist, so 'be a yogi'.
verses.reflection: Choose the yogi's path over the ascetic's, the scholar's, the ritualist's — be one, today, in spirit.
verses.background: The answer to Arjuna's doubt is complete: no effort in yoga is lost. Since this is so, as Śaṅkara puts it, Krishna now ranks the yogi against the other admired lives, the ascetic, the scholar of scripture and the performer of Vedic rites, and turns the ranking into a direct instruction to Arjuna.
verses.hook: Who stands higher than the ascetic, the scholar and the ritualist?

views.text: The 'knowers' here are those with scriptural learning, and the 'men of action' are those devoted to rites like the agnihotra; the yogi surpasses both.
Knowledge is the fruit of yoga, so the yogi stands above the learned; he stands above men of action because he alone knows how action should be done.
The ascetic disciplines body, speech and mind; the scholar has only indirect, book knowledge of the Self; the yogi has direct knowledge of it in deepest absorption.
Ascetics, scholars and ritualists still aim at worldly or bodily ends, while the yogi strives for God alone, so the yogi's attainment is on the spiritual plane and higher than theirs.

verses.devanagari:
योगिनामपि सर्वेषां मद्गतेनान्तरात्मना ।
श्रद्धावान्भजते यो मां स मे युक्ततमो मतः॥
verses.transliteration:
yogināmapi sarveṣāṃ madgatenāntarātmanā
śraddhāvānbhajate yo māṃ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ
verses.essence: And of all yogis, the one who worships me with faith, the inner self merged in me — that one I hold the most harnessed of all.
verses.translation: And among all the Yogis he who, full of faith and with his inner self merged in Me, worships Me is deemed by Me to be the most devout.

anvaya.parts: मद् (me) + गत (gone): that which has gone into me
अन्तर् (inner) + आत्मन् (self): the inner self

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (is regarded)

verses.explanation: One rung above 6.46's summit: among yogis themselves, the yuktatama — the most-united — is the one whose inner self has gone into Krishna (mad-gatena antarātmanā) and who worships him with faith. The chapter that opened with action free of craving, and climbed through posture, breath and stillness, ends with love: technique was the riverbed; devotion is the river. The superlative yukta-tamaḥ, most yoked, is awarded to intimacy, and that single word is the bridge to the chapters of devotion that follow.
verses.connection: Ranks within 6.46's yogis: highest is the one who worships Krishna with faith, mind merged in him, and 7.1 opens on how such a mind knows him.
verses.reflection: Of all your practices, let one today be done with inmost self gone to Him — the highest yoga.
verses.background: Krishna has just told Arjuna to become a yogi. One last distinction remains before chapter 6 ends: among yogis themselves, who stands highest. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as naming the devotee as best even among yogis given to discipline and restraint.
verses.hook: Among all kinds of yogis, which one does Krishna hold the highest?

refs.note: God says that though independent he becomes subject to his devotees, who conquer his heart; this is why the devotee ranks above every other yogi.
Among millions of liberated and perfected souls, a peaceful devotee of Narayan is very rare, supporting devotion as the highest attainment.

views.text: Among yogis meditating on deities like Rudra or Āditya, the one who worships Vāsudeva with faith is best; the chapter's teaching is said to culminate in the knowledge of 'Thou art That'.

'Among yogis' is read as 'than yogis': this lover of the Lord is beyond the four grades of 6.29-32, and the differences among other practitioners shrink to mustard seeds beside Mount Meru. He cannot bear a moment apart from the Lord.
Even among yogis devoted to restraints and observances, the Lord's devotee is the best; the implied counsel is: become My devotee.

This verse settles which yoga is highest: the bhakti yogi, because devotion binds God himself. Bhajate means loving service, so the devotee stands in the soul's natural place as God's eternal servant.
